description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](c37b0b21-3d11-46ea-ba5d-4be4c0caa8ae) as a replacement.**_
  
### Overview  
  
The Global Hunger Indices show the state of hunger worldwide in 2019, along with three reference years in 2000, 2005, and 2010. The indices capture the multidimensional nature of hunger by calculating Global Hunger Index (GHI) scores comprised of four indicators: undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting, and child mortality. 

  
  
The 2019 Global Hunger Index is published jointly by Concern Worldwide and Welthungerhilfe to measure and track hunger and to spotlight areas with the greatest need to eliminate hunger. The GHI scores are calculated on a 0-100 scale, where 0 indicates no hunger and 100 demonstrates complete hunger. A high GHI score, broadly speaking, can indicate a lack of food, a low-quality diet, insufficient child caregiving practices, an unhealthy environment, or all of these factors. The GHI classifies countries by the following severity layers: low, moderate, serious, alarming, or extremely alarming scales of hunger.   
  
### Methodology  
  
GHI scores were calculated using a three-step process that draws on available data from various sources to capture the multidimensional nature of hunger.
  
  

First, for each country, values were determined for four indicators:
  
  
1. Undernourishment: the share of the population that is undernourished (that is, whose caloric intake is insufficient);
  
  
2. Child wasting: the share of children under the age of five who are wasted (that is, who have low weight for their height, reflecting acute undernutrition);
  
  
3. Child stunting: the share of children under the age of five who are stunted (that is, who have low height for their age, reflecting chronic undernutrition); and
  
  
4. Child mortality: the mortality rate of children under the age of five (in part, a reflection of the fatal mix of inadequate nutrition and unhealthy environments).
  
  

Second, each of the four component indicators was given a standardized score on a 100-point scale based on the highest observed level for the indicator on a global scale in recent decades.
  
  

Third, standardized scores were aggregated to calculate the GHI score for each country, with each of the three dimensions (inadequate food supply, child mortality, and child undernutrition, which is composed equally of child stunting and child wasting) given equal weight.
  
  

This three-step process results in GHI scores on a 100-point GHI Severity Scale, where 0 is the best score (no hunger) and 100 is the worst. In practice, neither of these extremes is reached. A value of 0 would mean that a country had no undernourished people in the population, no children younger than five who were wasted or stunted, and no children who died before their fifth birthday. A value of 100 would signify that a country’s undernourishment, child wasting, child stunting, and child mortality levels were each at approximately the highest levels observed worldwide in recent decades. The GHI Severity Scale shows the severity of hunger - from low to extremely alarming - associated with the range of possible GHI scores.

title: Air Quality: Black Carbon Station Measurements
description:
### Overview  
  
The Air Quality: Black Carbon Station Measurements dataset is a global dataset that shows real-time air quality data from around the world for black carbon (BC). It presents data collected from government and international organizations at the station level. This means the data is more accurate to specific areas than national or regional data. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries and is being continually updated with new sources.

  
  
Black carbon is the sooty black material emitted from gas and diesel engines, coal-fired power plants, and other sources that burn fossil fuel. It is made up of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) that is 2.5 micrometers or less in diameter. PM2.5 can have significant health risks for people with compromised respiratory systems, the young, and the old. Black carbon is a global environmental problem that has negative implications for both human health and our climate. Inhalation of black carbon is associated with health problems including respiratory and cardiovascular disease, cancer, and even birth defects. Black carbon also contributes to climate change causing changes in patterns of rain and clouds.

  
  
OpenAQ is an open-source project to surface live, real-time air quality data from around the world. Its “mission is to enable previously impossible science, impact policy, and empower the public to fight air pollution.” Scientists, researchers, developers, and citizens can use these data to understand how air quality in different locations changes over time.

  
  
Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003anrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-25).  
  
### Methodology  
  
The black carbon station measurement dataset was produced and is continually updated by aggregating data from permanent outdoor air quality measures. Data was collected only from official sources, including government entities and international organizations. As of June 2017 OpenAQ data was available for 5,400 locations in 48 countries. For data to be included it had to meet three criteria:

  
  
1. The “raw” measurement data on physical particle concentration had to be available on the originating site.
  
  
2. The data needed to be at the “station level.” It is unacceptable if it is presented in an aggregated form for a city or region.
  
  
3. The data needed to be continuously updated at intervals between 10 minutes and 24 hours.

  
  
After the data was collected it was put into tables. Data was collected using the source organization’s Air Quality Index (AQI) classifications. The final dataset was mapped in vector format at a subnational level with each measurement station showing local particle concentration. OpenAQ continually reviews each data source website for updated values and updates the dataset every hour.

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows continually updated air quality data from OpenAQ on [inhalable particulates (PM10)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003bnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-10), [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cairqualityso2), [nitrogen dioxide (NO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003dnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-NO), [ozone (O₃)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003cnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-O), [carbon monoxide (CO)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003fnrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-CO), and [fine particulate matter (PM2.5)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/cit003anrt-Air-Quality-Measurements-PM-25).

Cropland and Pasture Area
description:
### Overview  
  
The Cropland and Pasture Area dataset shows the global distribution of agricultural activities for the year 2000. It is a combination of both satellite based datasets and agricultural inventory data from censuses. The dataset displays the percentage of land used for farming (cropland) and livestock (pasture area) for each grid cell. Each grid cell has a value of 0% to 100% coverage. A value of 0% means there are no agricultural activities present and 100% means the gridcell is completely used for cropland or pasture area. The dataset is displayed at a spatial resolution of 5 arc minutes (around 10 kilometers).
  
  

The Cropland and Pasture Area dataset was created by EarthStat with assistance from the University of Minnesota's Institute on the Environment (UMN IonE), and the Land Use and Global Environment Lab at the University of British Columbia (LUGE Lab at UBC). It was created to help understand the positive social and economic benefits, as well as the negative environmental consequences, of agricultural land use. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Cropland and Pasture Area in 2000 dataset was created by combining two different high-resolution satellite based land cover datasets and agricultural inventory data. The agricultural inventory data is allocated to the 10 kilometer resolution using the higher resolution land cover datasets and statistical modeling. 
  
  

The two satellite based land cover datasets used were the Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) Land Cover Type Product and the Satellite Pour l’Observation de la Terre (SPOT) VEGETATION based Global Land Cover 2000 (GLC2000) dataset. The MODIS dataset was created with data collected from October 2000 to October 2001 and was analyzed using remote imaging with a globally consistent classification scheme. The SPOT dataset was created with data from November 1999 to December 2000 and used a variable land use classification scheme that included information from regional institutions. Both datasets have a spatial resolution of about 1 kilometer. A single land cover dataset was created by overlaying the MODIS and GLC2000 datasets, where each classification was the combination of the MODIS and GLC2000 classifications. This combination land cover product was found to provide more accurate results when calibrated against the inventory data, as opposed to using either data set individually.
  
  

Cropland and pasture inventory data was compiled for the globe at the national and subnational level for circa year 2000. This resulted in compiled data for 15,990 different administrative units of the world, ranging from political units like countries, states and counties. Inventory data was found from either census data or the Food and Agriculture Organization's (FAO) [FAOSTAT database](http://faostat.fao.org). The cropland and pasture data was compiled to be consistent with the FAO definition of “Arable lands and permanent crops” and “Permanent pastures” respectively. The agricultural inventory data were seldom available exactly for the year 2000, therefore the authors collected inventory data between the years 1998 to 2002 where possible, but in several instances relied on older data.
  
  
 
Information within the final Cropland and Pasture Area dataset for areas that were clearly non-agricultural (tundra, boreal forest, and protected land) were masked to reduce the possibility of misclassification. For full information, please see the source [methodology](http://www.earthstat.org/cropland-pasture-area-2000/).

The goal of the Land-Use Harmonization (LUH2) project is to prepare a harmonized set of land-use scenarios that smoothly connects the historical reconstructions of land-use with the future projections in the format required for ESMs. The land-use harmonization strategy estimates the global fractional land-use patterns, underlying land-use transitions, and key agricultural management information, annually for the time period 850-2100 at 0.25° x 0.25° resolution, while minimizing the differences at the transition between the historical reconstruction ending conditions and IAM initial conditions, and working to preserve changes depicted by the IAMs in the future. description:
The GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP) was created by NASA's Goddard Institute for Space Studies (GISS) and is now run by NOAA's Earth System Research Laboratory Physical Sciences Division (ESRL-PSD). GISTEMP provides an estimate of global surface and air temperature changes. The basic GISS temperature analysis scheme was defined by James Hansen in the late 1970s, when a method of estimating global temperature change was needed for comparison with 1-dimensional global climate models. The scheme was based on the finding that the correlation of temperature change was reasonably strong for stations separated by up to 1,200 km, especially at middle and high latitudes. This fact proved sufficient to obtain useful estimates for global mean temperature changes. The analysis method was fully documented in Hansen and Lebedeff (1987), including quantitative estimates of the error in annual and 5-year mean temperature change. This was done by sampling at station locations a spatially complete data set of a long run of a global climate model, which was shown to have realistic spatial and temporal variability. This however only addresses the error due to incomplete spatial coverage of measurements. As there are other potential sources of error, such as urban warming near meteorological stations, many other methods have been used to verify the approximate magnitude of inferred global warming. These methods include inference of surface temperature change from vertical temperature profiles in the ground (bore holes) at many sites around the world, rate of glacier retreat at many locations, and studies by several groups of the effect of urban and other local human influences on the global temperature record. All of these yield consistent estimates of the approximate magnitude of global warming, which reached about 0.8°C in 2010, twice the magnitude reported in 1981. Further affirmation of the reality of the warming is its spatial distribution, which has largest values at locations remote from any local human influence, with a global pattern consistent with that expected for response to global climate forcings (larger in the Northern Hemisphere than the Southern Hemisphere, larger at high latitudes than low latitudes, larger over land than over ocean). More recent documentation compares alternative analyses and addresses questions about perception and reality of global warming; various choices for the ocean data are tested; it is also shown that global temperature change is sensitive to estimated temperature change in polar regions, where observations are limited. A multiyear smoothing is applied to fully remove the annual cycle and improve information content in temperature graphs. Despite large year-to-year fluctuations associated with the El Niño-La Niña cycle of tropical ocean temperature, the conclusion could be drawn that global temperature continued to rise rapidly in the 21st century, new record heights being reached in every decade. One of the improvements—introduced in 1998—was the implementation of a method to address the problem of urban warming: The urban and periurban (i.e., other than rural) stations are adjusted so that their long-term trend matches that of the mean of neighboring rural stations. Urban stations without nearby rural stations are dropped. This preserves local short-term variability without affecting long-term trends. Originally, the classification of stations was based on population size near that station; the current analysis uses satellite-observed night-lights to determine which stations are located in urban and periurban areas. Biodiversity Intactness
description:
### Overview  
  
The biodiversity intactness map shows global estimates of how land use pressures have affected the numbers of species and individuals found in an area. This data is important because if biodiversity loss goes unchecked, it will undermine efforts toward long-term sustainable development. The data, created by [Newbold et al. (2016)](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/353/6296/288), represents intactness in 2005 at a 1 kilometer resolution.   
  
### Methodology  
  
The Biodiversity Intactness dataset shows global estimates of how land use pressures have affected the numbers of species and individuals found in samples from local terrestrial ecological assemblages. The map represents the average losses of originally present species. The datasets used 2,382,624 data points from the Projecting Responses of Ecological Diversity in Changing Terrestrial Systems (PREDICTS) database, a global database of how local terrestrial biodiversity responds to human impacts. The map modeled how richness and abundance respond to land use pressures. The models included 4 pressure variables—land use, land use intensity, human population density, and proximity to the nearest road. The values of the response variables were expressed relative to an intact assemblage undisturbed by humans. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://science.sciencemag.org/content/353/6296/288).

description:
### Overview  
  
The FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index measures how restrictive foreign direct investment (FDI) is in a country. Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) is an investment made by an entity in one country into another country’s business interests. FDI is particularly important in developing countries and emerging markets as it can provide capital for technology and infrastructure and create jobs for local workers. However, some countries that receive foreign investment impose restrictions on FDI. For a given country, the four main FDI restrictions in each economic sector were evaluated and scored based on how discriminatory they are to foreign investors. These restrictions are foreign equity limitations; screening and approval requirements; restrictions on foreign key personnel; and other operational restrictions. Scores range from 0 (no restrictions) to 1 (full restrictions). The scores of each sector were averaged to calculate the country’s FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index. This dataset includes FDI data from 22 economic sectors for OECD and G20 countries and is updated annually.
  
  
The index captures a country’s ability to attract FDI. It can also be used to measure changes in regulatory restrictions over time and how these changes affect FDI inflow. Highly restrictive countries receive less FDI compared to less restrictive countries with similarly sized economies. FDI restrictions can be costly to governments in terms of loss of potential investments. They also increase costs in service sectors and negatively impact stocks. Studies of this dataset have shown that countries that reform FDI restrictions attract more foreign investors. FDI restrictions reform can positively impact developing countries by promoting economic growth and investment in human capital. 
  
  
The OECD created the FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index. The OECD is an international organization founded in 1961. The 36 member states work to shape policies that foster prosperity, equality, opportunity and well-being.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The FDI Regulatory Restrictions Index uses data from 22 economic sectors. Economic sectors include industries like agriculture, media, electricity, transportation and financial services. 
  
  
Scoring for each sector was based on the following restriction types:
Limits on the amount of foreign equity ownership permitted
Screening and approval procedures applied to inward foreign direct investment
Restrictions on the employment of foreigners as key personnel
Other restrictions (e.g., land ownership, reciprocity requirements, access to local finance)
  
  
Scoring was based on the discriminatory nature of a country’s measures, i.e. whether the measures applied to only foreign investors. Restrictions were evaluated on a 0 (no restrictions) to 1 (full restrictions) scale. The restrictiveness of each sector was calculated by adding the scores for each of the four types of FDI restrictions (with a maximum score of 1). A country’s FDI Regulatory Restrictiveness Index is the average of the scores from all 22 economic sectors. 

  
  
The score for **foreign equity limits** differentiated between three key thresholds: full exclusion of foreign participation, restrictions on foreign majority control and limits on full foreign ownership. The score further distinguished between start-up businesses and takeovers. If the measure only applied to takeovers, the score was reduced by half. **Screening and approval mechanisms** that applied only to foreign investors were scored based on a monetary threshold. Restrictive countries required approval of new FDI/acquisitions worth less than $100M U.S. or 50% of total equity. Less restrictive countries did not require approval of new FDI/acquisitions until they exceeded $100M U.S. or 50% of total equity. Open countries required no screening, only pre-notification from foreign investors. Restrictions on **foreign key personnel** were scored on two criteria: limitations on foreign employment and board of directors members. The OECD defines key personnel as employees in a managerial role or employees with essential technical skills. Restrictive countries did not allow employment of foreign key personnel. Less restrictive countries imposed time limits or required economic justification of foreign key personnel employment. Nationality/residence requirements for board of directors members are common. Restrictive countries required the majority of board members to be citizens. In contrast, less restrictive countries required only one board member to be a citizen. **Other restrictions** are measures that could affect the potential operations of foreign investors. These include restrictions on the following: land ownership, access to local finance, capital/profit repatriation, and establishment of local branches. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information

See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/com_007_rw1_fdi_regulatory_restrictiveness_index). title: Gender Inequality Index
description:
The Gender Inequality Index (GII), released by the UN Development Programme (UNDP), is an inequality index for 159 countries from 1995 to 2015. It measures gender inequalities and is calculated using 3 important aspects of human development: (1) reproductive health, measured by maternal mortality ratio and adolescent birth rates; (2) empowerment, measured by proportion of parliamentary seats occupied by females and proportion of adult females and males aged 25 years and older with at least some secondary education; and (3) economic status, expressed as labor market participation and measured by labor force participation rate of female and male populations aged 15 and older. The index ranges from 0, where women and men fare equally, to 1, where one gender fares as poorly as possible in all measured dimensions. The higher the GII value, the more disparities between females and males and the more loss to human development. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. Wastewater Plumes in Coastal Areas
description:
### Overview  
  
The Wastewater Plumes in Coastal Areas dataset, produced by National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis, models human sewage inputs into coastal waters for the year 2015. When human sewage flows into coastal waters it contributes to increased nitrogen levels and pathogens in coastal systems. This dataset quantifies and maps the flow of nitrogen and pathogen input to the ocean from nearly 135,000 watersheds using a high-resolution geospatial model. The sources of nitrogen inputs are separated by source into treated (sewered systems), septic, and untreated (open defecation) inputs. The dataset provides global rasters of the modeled plume, or extent, of the nitrogen in coastal waters. Nitrogen plume data is shown at ~1 km resolution. 

  
  
Human sewage is considered both an ecological and a human health issue because it contributes both increased levels of nitrogen and pathogens to coastal waters. Excess nitrogen plays a key role in the ecological degradation of coastal ecosystems through a process called [eutrophication](https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/eutrophication.html). Eutrophication leads to harmful algal blooms and low-oxygen waters, which can kill fish, and degrade essential fish habitats. Pathogens in coastal waters can promote disease in marine organisms, such as coral reefs, and can cause human health impacts. It is important to monitor both nitrogen and pathogen concentrations, to understand trends and inform management.  

  
  
The National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis created this dataset to inform marine conservation and public health work. The model allows for the comparison of global models of nitrogen sources with traditional water quality monitoring to identify priority hotspots. In-depth local monitoring can then pinpoint the true sources of and quantities of pollutants like nitrogen to benefit conservation and management. The model also links nitrogen inputs with data on pathogens in coastal waters to inform policy decisions around wastewater treatment options. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Nitrogen concentration (grams/yr) was modeled using a high-resolution geospatial model. Population and settlement data were grouped into rural and urban classes. These data were then combined with national-level statistics on protein consumption and the proportion of the population’s access to various types of wastewater treatment facilities. Wastewater treatment types were grouped into three categories - open defecation (untreated), septic tanks (septic), or some level of sewered treatment. The three sewage treatment categories of nitrogen were assigned a nitrogen removal efficiency based on literature. The model assumed that populations with inputs from septic tanks or open defecation that are more than 1km away from surface waters and coastlines do not contribute to effluent totals. 

  
  
The dispersion of the wastewater pollution into the ocean was then modeled from each basin’s pourpoint, which describes the location where freshwater enters the ocean. For each watershed with a pourpoint draining into the ocean, nitrogen inputs were calculated by summing the values for all grid cells falling within the watershed boundary and this value was assigned to the corresponding coastal pourpoint. At each pourpoint, the level of nitrogen was spread into the coastal waters using a plume model based on a logarithmic decay function. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0258898#sec002).
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also provides data on nitrogen inputs at the watershed level in [Watersheds Transporting Wastewater to Coastal Ocean](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/784732cc-8e7e-4dac-be51-d4506ff2ee04) and for the associated coastal “pourpoint” or the location where the watershed empties into the ocean in  [Wastewater Inputs to Coastal Areas](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/5bf349ec-3b14-4021-a7d4-fc4b8104bd74).

title: U.S. Projected Change in Number of Days over 90º - Higher Emissions (2041-2070)
description:
These data were used to create Figure 16.2 in the Third National Climate Assessment report.
See: http://nca2014.globalchange.gov/report/regions/northeast#graphic-17071
 
This figure shows the average of projections of the number of days over 90 degrees Fahrenheit from several climate models. On the global scale, climate model simulations show consistent projections of future temperature conditions under a range of emissions scenarios. All models show warming by late this century that is much larger than historical variations nearly everywhere globally. For the U.S., models unequivocally project large and historically unprecedented future warming in every region of the U.S. under all of the scenarios used in this assessment. The amount of warming varies substantially between higher versus lower scenarios, and moderately from model to model, but the amount of projected warming is much larger than historical variations. Likewise, the models project unequivocal increases in the number of days over 90 degrees Fahrenheit that are larger than historical variations.
 
Dataset:
1/8 degree-CONUS Daily Downscaled Climate Projections by Katharine Hayhoe: https://cida.usgs.gov/thredds/catalog.html
Multi-model mean annual number of days above 90oF under both a high (A2) and low (B1) emissions scenario, for the period 2041-2070.
 
Models: Used to calculate the multi-model means: cgcm3_t47, cgcm3_t63, cnrm, echam5, gfdl_2.1, pcm
 
Indicators:
tmax90oF: Annual number of days above 90oF (based on daily maximum temperature)
 
Emission Scenarios
SRES emissions scenarios: a2, b1
 
Time periods: 30-year averages: 2041-2070

Fishing Activity
description:
### Overview  
  
The Apparent Fishing Effort dataset, produced by Global Fishing Watch (GFW), shows the distribution of time spent fishing in different locations throughout the ocean at a 0.01 degree resolution between 2012 and 2021. The time spent fishing in each pixel is tracked using a maritime Automatic Identification System (AIS).

  
  
Commercial fishing is a vital part of the global economy and is crucial to the food security and cultural identity of millions of people. However some practices, like trawling and dredging, destroy far more ocean habitat than any other fishing practice. When dredging or trawling, commercial vessels drag a dredge or heavy net, respectively, along the seafloor to scrape up species like oysters or shrimp. The process of scraping the seafloor is extremely destructive to deep-sea marine ecosystems, productivity, biodiversity, and carbon storage. Historically, practices like trawling and dredging have been difficult and costly to monitor, but technology and transparency are driving tangible change in how the sector is managed. 

  
  
Global Fishing Watch is advancing ocean governance through increased transparency of human activity at sea. By creating and publicly sharing map visualizations, data and analysis tools, they enable scientific research and drive a transformation in how we manage our ocean. By 2030, they aim to monitor and visualize the impact of ocean-going vessels, both industrial and small-scale, that are responsible for the vast majority of the global seafood catch.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Global Fishing Watch’s apparent fishing effort dataset is based on transmissions broadcast using publicly available automatic identification system (AIS) information. AIS is a GPS-like device that large ships use to broadcast their position in order to avoid collisions. Each year, more than 400,000 AIS devices broadcast vessel location along with other information on vessel identity, course and speed. Ground stations and satellites pick up this information, meaning a ship’s movements can be followed even in the most remote parts of the ocean. 

  
  
GFW uses two convolutional neural networks (CNN)—a cutting edge form of machine learning model—to help classify fishing vessels (vessel characterization model) and predict when they are fishing (fishing detection model). They first [identify fishing vessels](https://globalfishingwatch.org/datasets-and-code-vessel-identity/) by combining a comprehensive database of vessel registry information with the output of the vessel characterization model to predict features like geartype and size. Next, GFW estimates where and when each vessel is fishing based on its movement patterns. The fishing detection model was trained using over a thousand manually labeled vessel tracks to learn what fishing movements look like. This model predicts a score for every AIS position in the database to distinguish fishing positions from non-fishing positions, such as during vessel transits. When the fishing detection model scores an AIS position as a fishing position, the time associated with that AIS position is considered apparent fishing activity. For more information about the two models, please see the supplementary materials of the [associated paper](https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.aao5646).

  
  
After identifying fishing vessels and detecting fishing positions in the AIS data, apparent fishing effort can be calculated for any area by summarizing the fishing hours for all fishing vessels in that area. Global Fishing Watch’s fishing detection algorithm is a best effort mathematically to identify “apparent fishing activity.” As a result, it is possible that some fishing activity is not identified as such by Global Fishing Watch; conversely, Global Fishing Watch may show apparent fishing activity where fishing is not actually taking place. 

  
  
 To generate maps of apparent fishing effort GFW “rasterizes” the AIS positions by placing them into a grid and calculating the total fishing activity in each grid cell. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.aao5646)
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. This map displays effort by all vessels other than trawlers or dredgers. Resource Watch shows separate GFW data for [Trawling Activity](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/6ccfb266-20cd-4838-82b0-5309987a62f0). [Data disaggregated by flag state, vessel, and gear type](https://globalfishingwatch.org/data-download/datasets/public-fishing-effort) is also available through Global Fishing Watch. 

  
  
For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team requested a visualization of the data through the Global Fishing Watch API. This visualization powered by 4-Wings, Global Fishing Watch experimental technology for rapid access to global
scale temporal data sets. See the documentation on how Resource Watch retrieved the data on [Github.](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/com_030a_rw1_fishing_activity)

Annual Precipitation
description:
The Annual Precipitation data set was adapted from the University of California, Berkeley's WorldClim V1 Bioclim, which produces bioclimatic variables derived from the monthly temperature and rainfall in order to generate more biologically meaningful values. The data product covers the period January 1, 1960, to December 31, 1990, and has global coverage at 1 km resolution. The bioclimatic variables represent annual trends (e.g., mean annual temperature, annual precipitation), seasonality (e.g., annual range in temperature and precipitation), and extreme or limiting environmental factors (e.g., temperature of the coldest and warmest month, and precipitation of the wettest and driest quarters). Climate data sets were created based on data from various sources, including the Global Historical Climate Network data set, the World Meteorological Organization's Climatological Normals (CLINO), the FAOCLIM 2.0 global climate database, the International Center for Tropical Agriculture, and various regional climate databases. The data set contains the following bands: Annual Mean Temperature; Mean Diurnal Range; Isothermality; Temperature Seasonality; Max Temperature of Warmest Month; Min Temperature of Coldest Month; Temperature Annual Range; Mean Temperature of Wettest Quarter; Mean Temperature of Driest Quarter; Mean Temperature of Warmest Quarter; Mean Temperature of Coldest Quarter; Annual Precipitation; Precipitation of Wettest Month (mm); Precipitation of Driest Month (mm); Precipitation Seasonality; Precipitation of Wettest Quarter (mm); Precipitation of Driest Quarter (mm); Precipitation of Warmest Quarter (mm); and Precipitation of Coldest Quarter (mm). This scheme follows that of ANUCLIM, except that for temperature seasonality the standard deviation was used because a coefficient of variation does not make sense with temperatures between -1 and 1. title: Positive Peace Index
description:
### Overview  
  
The Positive Peace Index (PPI) is a quantitative approach to measure Positive Peace. Positive Peace is defined as the attitudes, institutions, and structures that lead to a more peaceful society. A country with a higher PPI is more capable of building and maintaining peace. 

  
  
The Positive Peace Index dataset was created by the Institute for Economics & Peace to measure a country’s success in building and maintaining peace.  Positive peace is used to create resilient and adaptive communities that prevent conflict and help societies channel disagreements productively. The framework for PPI is based on eight domains:

  
  
1. *Acceptance of the Rights of Others:* This requires countries to have formal laws that can guarantee basic human rights and freedoms, ensure gender equality, and worker’s rights.
  
  
2. *Equitable Distribution of Resources:* This ensures everyone has equal access to resources, such as education and health.
  
  
3. *Free Flow of Information:* This is measured by the extent to which citizens can gain access to information, whether the media is free and independent, and how well-informed citizens are.
  
  
4. *Good Relations with Neighbours:* A country’s relationship with other countries is an important indicator of how peaceful and politically stable the country is.
  
  
5. *High Levels of Human Capital:*  The employment rate among young citizens and the number of people engaged in research activities shows the level of social capital in a country.
  
  
6. *Low Levels of Corruption:*  High levels of corruption leads to a shortage of funding for essential services, which creates unrest in a society.
  
  
7. *Sound Business Environment:*  This is measured by the presence of regulatory systems and formal institutions in a country to support a good business environment.
  
  
8. *Well-Functioning Government:*  A government that delivers high-quality public and civil services, creates trust and participation, maintains political stability, and promotes the rule of law is necessary for a peaceful country.

  
  
The PPI data is reported at a national level with global coverage. Data is updated annually and is available from 2009 to 2018 for 163 countries covering 99.6% of the world’s population. This data can help to understand and make progress towards global peacefulness along with other interrelated areas such as:  improved economic productivity and social advancement.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Positive Peace Index (PPI) uses 24 indicators in eight domains to measure Positive Peace. The eight domains range from the flow of information within a country to levels of corruption. PPI is interconnected to the Global Peace Index (GPI) which is another measurement for global peacefulness. GPI is a quantification of the absence of violence or the fear of violence in a country. The internal measures of the Global Peace Index were statistically compared to approximately 25,000 national data series, indices, and attitudinal surveys to determine the initial set of indicators for Positive Peace Index. These indicators were then qualitatively assessed. If there were multiple indicators for similar cases, the least important ones were discarded. 

  
  
Finally, the remaining indicators were aggregated into the eight domains of Positive Peace and given a correlation coefficient to their value in GPI using statistical approaches. The correlation coefficient represented how important the indicators were in the PPI measurement compared to GPI. The correlation coefficient was used to weight GPI Internal Peace scores for each indicator and create a final score out of 5.  For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://visionofhumanity.org/app/uploads/2019/10/PPR-2019-web.pdf).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data

See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/soc_092_positive_peace_index). title: India Projected Change in Average Temperature
description:
This dataset, available from the Centre for Climate Change Research (CCCR) at the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM), shows projected change in average temperature over the Indian subcontinent. 

These downscaled climate scenarios contain high resolution downscaled projections of regional climate and monsoon over South Asia until 2100 for the IPCC using the International Centre for Theoretical Physics (ICTP) Regional Climate Model (RegCM4) at 50 km horizontal resolution. The projections are an ensemble of six member global climate models from the CMIP5, which help drive the regional model with lateral and lower boundary conditions. The IITM-RegCM4 regional climate model outputs are archived by CCCR-IITM in the framework of the WCRP regional activity Coordinated Regional Climate Downscaling Experiment (CORDEX; http://www.cordex.org), and are disseminated to users and stakeholders for application studies and impact assessments by publishing on the CCCR-IITM Earth System Grid Federation (ESGF) data node (see more details at http://cccr.tropmet.res.in/home/cordexsa_datasets.jsp).

Projected change in average temperature is computed using daily mean near-surface air temperature in degrees Celsius for the historical period (1951-2005) and for future projections (2006-2099) based on two Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) scenarios (RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5) of the IPCC. These indicators are then used to derive an ensemble mean (average of the 6 IITM-RegCM4 model members). These are presented as the future changes in three 30-year period: short-term (2016-2045), mid-term (2036-2065), and long-term (2066-2095) averages relative to the baseline 30-year period (1976-2005) average.

The daily fields from 1951 to 2099 for each member model available in netCDF4 file format are processed to compute the climate indicators (30-year averages) using the Climate Data Operators (CDO; https://code.mpimet.mpg.de/projects/cdo), which is a collection of command line operators to manipulate and analyze climate model data. The processed climate indicators available in netCDF4 file format can be visualized using the Grid Analysis and Display System (GrADS; http://cola.gmu.edu/grads), an interactive desktop tool that is used for easy access, manipulation, and visualization of earth science data.

description: The NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP) dataset is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP dataset includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5 from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. title: Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation Days U.S. (RCP8.5)
description:
The Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average days of extreme precipitation at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. An extreme precipitation day is defined as a day where precipitation is greater than the 99th percentile precipitation compared to the baseline period. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the number of extreme precipitation days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual number of extreme precipitation days between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Days of extreme precipitation are divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change. Values greater than 1 indicate that extreme precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. Data is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and the resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation dataset provides projections on how extreme precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. Generally, extreme precipitation events are expected to become more frequent worldwide. 

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Extreme Precipitation dataset was created with precipitation data from LOCA. The LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference.  

The annual average extreme precipitation days for each year, climate model, and scenario were calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by extracting the daily precipitation values for a given year and summing the number of days where precipitation was greater than the 99th percentile precipitation during the baseline period. The annual average extreme precipitation days were combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in extreme precipitation. Values greater than 1 indicate that extreme precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing.

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the extreme precipitation days in 2000 is actually an average of the annual extreme precipitation days between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.
temporal_start_raw: Baseline period of 1960-1990 and projected values for each decade 2000 to 2080

description: GADM is a spatial database of the location of the world's administrative areas (or adminstrative boundaries) for use in GIS and similar software. Administrative areas in this database are countries and lower level subdivisions such as provinces, departments, counties, etc. GADM describes where these administrative areas are (the spatial features), and for each area it provides some attributes, such as the name and variant names.

title: Soil Erosion
description:
### Overview  
  
The Soil Erosion Prevalence dataset, produced by the World Agroforestry Centre (ICRAF), provides predictions for the percentage of area with soil erosion across the global tropics (between the parallels of 40° south and 40° north). The authors predicted soil erosion for the years 2002, 2007, 2012, 2017, and 2020 from satellite imagery at 500 m resolution using machine learning algorithms trained with field observations. 

  
  
Soil is eroding more quickly than its being formed, contributing to the degradation of millions of hectares of land globally. The nutrient rich layer of soil on the surface, called topsoil, is vulnerable to wind and water erosion and its loss is accelerated by modifications in land use. Erosion of this critical layer of soil comes at a [major economic and environmental cost](https://www.wri.org/insights/causes-and-effects-soil-erosion-and-how-prevent-it). It causes [billions](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0264837718319343) of dollars of losses due to decreased soil fertility, reduced crop yields, and increased water usage. The eroded soil can be carried into rivers and streams. This creates a heavy layer of sediment which is carried downstream. This process clogs waterways, prevents smooth water flow, and may eventually lead to flooding. Other environmental costs include loss of productivity and biodiversity, decreased resilience of marine and terrestrial ecosystems, and increased vulnerability to climate change and food insecurity. 

  
  
Estimates of both spatial and temporal dynamics of soil erosion are needed to better track the occurrence and severity of erosion in landscapes over time. The main objectives of this dataset are to provide rapid assessments of soil erosion for spatially distributed monitoring as well as assess changes in soil erosion prevalence over time. The spatial assessments of erosion provide estimates of land degradation hotspots and can be combined with other indicators of ecosystem health, including social factors, to better assess and identify drivers of land degradation and target land management interventions to reverse degradation.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
The authors used a combination of systematically collected field observations of erosion and remote sensing to predict the spatial and temporal distribution of soil erosion prevalence at moderate spatial resolution (500 m) for the years 2002, 2007, 2012, 2017, and 2020. The model was trained and tested using field data collected via [the Land Degradation Surveillance Framework](http://landscapeportal.org/blog/2015/03/25/the-land-degradation-surveillance-framework-ldsf) (LDSF). As part of the LDSF, sample sites are divided into plots and subplots. Erosion prevalence was scored at the plot level by summing up the number of subplots with visible signs of erosion, with 0 being no observed erosion and 4 being erosion observed in all four subplots. The authors took a cut-off at three subplots or more (>50%) to represent “severe” soil erosion. Erosion prevalence was modeled using a decision-tree approach known as [Random Forests](https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v077i01/v77i01.pdf) to generate a classification model for soil erosion prevalence using imagery from the [Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiomer](https://modis.gsfc.nasa.gov/data/) (MODIS) platform. Annual composites were matched to the years of LDSF field data collection and fitted to annual composite reflectance data for 2002, 2007, 2012, and 2017. Soil erosion prevalence is displayed on the maps as the percentage of area (of a pixel) predicted to be eroded. Model accuracy for the detection of erosion was about 86% and accuracy for non-detection was about 91%.

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-4292/11/15/1800).

title: Population (Grid, 1 km)
description:
The Gridded Population of the World, Version 4 (GPW v4), Population Density Adjusted to Match 2015 Revision of UN WPP Country Totals, produced by SEDAC, consists of estimates of human population density, based on counts consistent with national censuses and population registers with respect to relative spatial distribution but adjusted to match the 2015 revision of UN World Population Prospects country totals for the years 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, and 2020. A proportional allocation gridding algorithm, utilizing approximately 12.5 million national and subnational administrative units, is used to assign population values to 30 arc-second (~1 km) grid cells. The population density grids are derived by dividing the population count grids by the land area grids. The pixel values represent people per km2.

title: Maximum Arctic Sea Ice
description:
### Overview  
  
The Maximum Arctic Sea Ice dataset shows the annual maximum extent of sea ice in the Arctic for select years between 1980-2020. Arctic sea ice typically reaches its maximum extent in March. In this map, light blue represents locations where sea ice was present during March for each year. Sea ice extent data was collected by satellite microwave sensing instruments at a spatial resolution of 25 kilometers (km). This dataset is derived from two products: a near real-time daily dataset and a separate daily dataset that is processed yearly. For the most recent 6-18 months, sea ice extents were derived from near real-time data; all older data was derived from the separate daily dataset. 

  
  
This dataset can be used to understand changes in annual maximum Arctic sea ice extent over the past 40 years. Arctic sea ice extent has been declining since 2000. Melting sea ice can have [dramatic effects on global climate](https://nsidc.org/cryosphere/seaice/environment/global_climate.html). Because of its white color, sea ice reflects sunlight back into space. This property – albedo – keeps the polar regions cold. However, as sea ice continues to melt, the Earth’s surface absorbs more sunlight, causing an increase in temperature and ice melt. When sea ice melts, it changes the ocean’s salinity and temperature, disrupting currents and weather patterns. 

  
  
The [National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC)](https://nsidc.org/) was founded in 1976 as the World Data Center for Glaciology. Over time, the NSIDC evolved to become a data distribution and research center specializing in remote sensing of cryospheric data such as snow, sea ice, frozen ground, ice sheets and glaciers. In addition to managing and distributing this data, the NSIDC creates and supports data access tools for its users. They also use the datasets for climate research and education. The NSIDC is part of University of Colorado Boulder’s [Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences (CIRES)](https://cires.colorado.edu/). It is supported by the [National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA)](https://www.nasa.gov/), the [National Science Foundation (NSF)](https://www.nsf.gov/) and the [National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)](https://www.noaa.gov/).  
  
### Methodology  
  
Maximum Arctic Sea Ice was produced from two sources: NASA's [Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC)](https://nsidc.org/data/nsidc-0051) and NSIDC’s [Near-Real-Time DMSP SSMIS Daily Polar Gridded Sea Ice Concentrations (NRTSI)](https://nsidc.org/data/nsidc-0081).

  
  
Data for the GSFC and NRTSI datasets was collected by the following six sensors:
- GSFC data:
  - [Nimbus-7 Satellite](https://eospso.nasa.gov/missions/nimbus-7) Scanning Multichannel Microwave Radiometer (SMMR) from October 1978 to August 1987
  - [Defense Meteorological Satellite Program (DMSP)](https://www.ospo.noaa.gov/Operations/DMSP/index.html) F8 Special Sensor Microwave/Imager (SSM/I) from August 1987 to December 1991
  - DMSP-F11 SSM/I from December 1991 to September 1995
  - DMSP-F13 SSM/I from September 1995 to December 2007
  - DMSP-F17 Special Sensor Microwave Imager/Sounder (SSMIS) from January 2008 to present
- NRTSI data:
  - DMSP-F18 SSMIS from April 2016 to present

  
  
The SMMR, SSM/I, and SSMIS instruments sense emitted microwave radiation. Data was collected daily by the SSM/I and SSMIS sensors and on alternate days by the SMMR sensor. An object's physical properties, such as atomic composition and crystalline structure, determine the amount of microwave radiation it emits. The crystalline structure of ice typically emits more microwave energy than liquid ocean water. Thus, the microwave sensors can easily distinguish sea ice from the ocean. The satellite data was converted to [brightness temperature](https://glossary.ametsoc.org/wiki/Brightness_temperature), a descriptive measure of an object's radiation. Brightness temperature data was then converted to gridded ice concentration using the [NASA Team algorithm](https://nsidc.org/support/faq/nasa-team-vs-bootstrap-algorithm#NASATeam1) at a spatial resolution of 25 km. Gridded ice concentration is the percentage of ice (relative to water) in a given cell. Each cell’s daily ice concentrations were averaged to produce monthly concentrations. 

  
  
Sea ice extent is delineated by the location where ice ends and water (open ocean) begins. Cells were classified as water if their average monthly ice concentration was below 15%, and as ice if the concentration was above 15%. Images of sea ice extent were created for each month, with ice shown in light blue. The process was the same for both the NRTSI and GSFC datasets. 

  
  
GSFC data had a tighter quality control than NRTSI data. However, GSFC data is only released once per year. NRTSI data was available at the end of each month, so it was used to produce sea ice extents while GSFC data was being processed. GSFC data replaced NRTSI data once it was available. Thus, data from the most recent 6-18 months was derived from the NRTSI dataset and older data was derived from the GSFC dataset. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows additional NSIDC sea ice extent data: [Historical Sea Ice Medians](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/b1ebea96-5963-4c2c-9273-7d08536ac07d), [Minimum Arctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/a99c5cf5-f141-4bed-a36d-b04c8e171dfa), [Arctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/484fbba1-ac34-402f-8623-7b1cc9c34f17), [Minimum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/05fd2614-325b-460a-8b52-3155fa9dd98f), [Maximum Antarctic Sea Ice](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/7667bdd8-9adb-44de-b51c-d2d26e461af1) and [Antarctic Sea Ice Extent](http://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/e740efec-c673-431a-be2c-b214613f641a).

Flood Events
description:
### Overview  
  
The Flood Events dataset shows major flood events within the last month. This near real-time dataset is created using data from news articles and government sources. While the map only shows the location and extent for floods within the last month, additional information on flood start and end dates, number of deaths, number of people displaced, main cause, and severity are all available in the Custom Visualization tool below. 

  
  
According to the [United Nations](https://www.unenvironment.org/news-and-stories/story/how-climate-change-making-record-breaking-floods-new-normal), floods will become more likely due to global climate change. They can have large consequences for civil society including the loss of life, damage to property, and increasing health risks. This dataset lets viewers monitor where flooding is happening around the world on a near real-time basis. It can also offer a first glance at the communities that have been impacted by flooding. Lastly, it can help government agencies in creating natural disaster management plans and zoning for future urbanization.

  
  
This dataset was created and is curated by the Dartmouth Flood Observatory located at the University of Colorado’s Institute of Arctic and Alpine Research (INSTAAR). It is a continually updated archive that can show trends in severity, damage, and location of flood events.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
This dataset was created and is continually updated with information from a wide array of news and government sources, like the North American Atmospheric and Oceanic Administration’s National Climatic Data Center (NOAA NCDC). To identify each flood, researchers used the international [Global Identified Number](https://glidenumber.net/glide/public/search/search.jsp) (GLIDE), which is a unique ID code used to identify disasters that is issued by the [Emergency Events Database (EM-DAT)](https://www.emdat.be/) at the Centre for Research on the Epidemiology of Disasters (CRED).

  
  
For each flood, event data on location, size, begin & end times, duration, deaths, number of people displaced, main cause, and severity were recorded. Size, times, duration, main cause, and location are all taken directly from the source. Number of deaths were taken from news and government sources when accurate enough, but when only a range of numbers were provided by these sources researchers estimated that “hundreds” meant more than 300 people had died, “more than 100” meant 110 or more had died, and “scores” meant more than 30 people had died. Number of people displaced was based on the quantity of people left homeless after the incident and sometimes the number evacuated during the flood. Severity was determined by reviewing the amount of damage caused by the event and how often similar events have occured in the region.

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://floodobservatory.colorado.edu/Archives/ArchiveNotes.html).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Data on flood events for every year between 1985 and present are available from the data provider. Additionally, the data provider also has datasets on river and reservoir discharge, flood and drought-affected watersheds, and precipitation. An interactive map can also be found on the source website. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/wat_040_flood_events)

title: Marine Species Richness
description: To calculate the impact of climate change on marine biodiversity, researchers first determined biodiversity distribution ranging from 0 (absence of species) to 1 (maximum species richness) (Ramirez et al. 2017). They calculated the species richness distribution based on the spatially explicit information on the equally weighted distribution of fish (1,729), marine mammal (124), and seabird (330) species. Data on the world distribution species are from BirdLife International (http://www.birdlife.org) and the International Union for Conservation of Nature (http://www.iucnredlist.org/). Occurrence shapefiles were transformed to 0.5 degree, dichotomous grid features, with 1 denoting presence and 0 indicating absences. Obtained grid features for different fish, marine mammal, and seabird species were added to obtain 3 maps indicating the number of species per group occurring in each pixel. Each map was standardized by the total number of species per group in order to obtain a relative measure of the spatial distribution of fish, marine mammal, and seabird species richness. These relative values were subsequently added on a pixel basis and standardized again to the maximum value to obtain a dimensionless index ranging from 0 (absence of species) to 1 (maximum species richness), providing information about the spatial heterogeneity in species richness and highlighting hotspots of marine biodiversity without biases toward those groups (e.g., fish) with a larger number of species. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.

Extreme Heat Days
description:
Extreme heat days represent the annual average count of days with heat greater than the 99th percentile of the baseline, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). 

The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100.

The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run).

The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm 
 
PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

Projected Cooling Degree Days U.S. (RCP8.5)
description:
The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual cooling degree days (CDDs) at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. CDD is the number of degrees that a day's average temperature is above 65 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). For example, if a day's average temperature is 80°F, the CDD would be 15. If this happened 10 times in a year the annual CDD would be 150. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. CDD projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades and how this may affect future energy demands. For example, CDD is often used as a proxy to estimate energy requirements for cooling buildings. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset was created with temperature data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference.  

The annual CDD for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. Daily CDDs were calculated by subtracting the baseline temperature of 65°F from daily average temperature values. If the daily average temperature was below 65°F, it was counted as zero. Then, annual CDD was calculated by summing all daily CDD values over a given year. Annual CDDs were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in cooling degree days.

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

Current and Projected Food Insecurity
description: The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) Food Security Outlook shapefiles are created by FEWS NET, led by U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID), U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), National Aeronautic and Space Administration (NASA), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Kimetrica, and Chemonics. Food security for a region is determined according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification approach. This is a standardized approach to classifying the level of food insecurity in a region. Classifications are typically released 4 times a year, each with a short-term (0-3 months from publication) and medium-term (4-7 months from publication) evaluation of food insecurity at the subnational level. The approach revolves around a consensus-building process. Food security experts review the available evidence to determine a food security classification on a scale of 1 to 5, with phase 1 corresponding to minimal food insecurity, and phase 5 corresponding to famine-level food insecurity. Evidence used includes satellite data measuring precipitation anomalies (CHIRPS SPI), vegetation anomalies (NDVI), and expert opinion based on knowledge of market and trade functioning and socioeconomic dynamics in each region of interest, among others. The data covers select regions from East, West, and Central Africa, Central America, and Afghanistan. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. For access to the full dataset and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: [Archived] Cooling Degree Days (Decadal)
description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](6fa000b5-8d91-46c8-8502-07427bc5eafc) as a replacement.**_
  
A cooling degree day (CDD) is defined as the number of degrees that a day's mean temperature is above 65°F. For example, if a day's average temperature is 80°F, the CDD would be 15. If a second day's average temperature were the same, the combined CDD for those two days would be 30. CDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate heating and cooling needs in buildings. While degree days can be calculated using any reference temperature, this data set uses 65°F (18.3°C), a common threshold for climate indicators, and a temperature at which people are generally comfortable. 

This indicator is useful in determining energy demands resulting from cooling in different regions and assessing projected climate change impacts.

This Cooling Degree Days data set shows CDDs for decades between 1971-2090 under RCP 8.5, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP).

The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5 from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100. 

The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run). 

The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on Resource Watch. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. title: U.S. Climate Resilience
description:
The Climate Resilience Screening Index (CRSI), developed by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), characterizes U.S. county and community resilience based on a suite of indicators that are grouped into broad categories of county and community resiliency traits in the context of natural disasters. The index is a composite measure comprised of five domains (Risk, Governance, Society, Built Environment, and Natural Environment), represented by 20 indicators, and calculated from 117 metrics. CRSI characterizes holistic climate resilience throughout the U.S. at the county level (2000-2015); ascertains the relationships among those domains and indicators; and provides information regarding how that resilience score is constructed and the actions a community/county can take to improve their climate resilience. CRSI is intended to be used by EPA Regions and others who work closely with counties and communities to gauge resilience of built and natural systems to acute climate events (e.g., hurricanes, wildfires, tornadoes, flooding).

This dataset includes the percentage of the population with access to electricity from 1990 to present, at the country level. The data represents electricity access in the urban population of each country.
  
  
Access to electricity is crucial to improving the standard of living and is one of the most obvious indications of a country’s energy poverty status. Securing electricity services while decarbonizing power systems is a key challenge for developing countries, as electricity generation from fossil fuels contributes to climate change.

  
  
While this dataset shows access to electricity at the national level, Resource Watch also shows data for the percentage of [rural](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene012b-Access-to-Electricity-Rural) and [national](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/ene012a-Access-to-Electricity) population with access to electricity.
