title: Biodiversity Hotspots
description: First defined in 1988 by scientist Norman Myers, biodiversity hotspots are areas characterized by high levels of endemic plants coupled with significant habitat loss. Endemism is the ecological state of a species being unique to a defined geographic location, such as an island, nation, country or other defined zone, or habitat type. Specifically, a region must meet the following criteria to achieve the hotspot classification formulated by Conservation International (CI): (1) at least 1,500 species of vascular plants (>0.5% of the world’s total) are endemic; and (2) at least 70% of the original natural vegetation has been lost. When Myers first defined the term, he identified 10 tropical forest hotspots. The need to pinpoint priority conservation regions led CI to adopt the term and reassess the hotspot concept. In this process, CI introduced quantitative thresholds (see above) and added additional regions. At that time, there were 25 hotspots. Because of the constant change in environmental threats and the improved understanding of biodiversity, CI has since revisited the hotspots to refine boundaries, update information, and add new regions to create this global data set. This process produced an additional 10 hotspots, bringing the total to 35. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

title: Electricity Installed Capacity
description:
### Overview  
  
Electricity installed capacity measures the [maximum electric output](https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=101&t=3) an electricity generator can produce under specific conditions. This dataset reveals the amount of electricity all the power plants in a country can produce within a year and helps quantify the [growth of energy resources](https://www.energy.gov/ne/articles/what-generation-capacity). However, considering many generators do not operate at their full capacity all the time, a generator's actual electric output [varies based on conditions at the power plant, fuel costs, and/or as instructed by the electric power grid operator](https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=101&t=3). Therefore, this dataset represents the theoretical electricity output that is possible, rather than the actual electricity generation.
  
  

The Electricity Installed Capacity dataset was released by the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA). This data was reported at a national level with global coverage. Data is available for the years 1980-2019, though most countries only have data for a subset of these years. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
EIA compiled data from a list of external sources including  
- International Energy Agency (IEA)
- Power Reactor Information System (PRIS) from International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA)
- Platts World Power Plants Database
- International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA)
- International Hydropower Association (IHA)
- United Nations (UN) Energy Statistics Database
- BP Statistical Review of World Energy
- Other government agencies, research institutes, and companies
  
  

Electricity data shows the capacity as of December 31 each year. Data from both utility and non-utility sources was used. EIA is in the process of creating specific country-level metadata for this dataset. For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button. 
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows the [Total Energy Consumption](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/67cf410f-4cdf-4437-aa09-187e5fa590ae) dataset and [Electricity Consumption] (https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/eef10736-8d8b-4ac9-a715-ef0653a83196) dataset by EIA.
  
  

Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data for the electricity installed capacity of different energy resources from 1980 through 2018 is available from the data provider. 

For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

Each file covers a calendar month and the mean values provided are simply the arithmetic means of the individual CO₂ retrievals which fall within that grid box over the month. The midtropospheric CO₂ retrievals have been averaged and binned into 2.5 x 2 degree grid cells, from -180.0 to +180.0 degrees longitude and from -60.0 to +90.0 degrees latitude. description:
The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset shows the change in annual cooling degree days (CDDs) at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. CDD is the number of degrees that a day's average temperature is above 65 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). For example, if a day's average temperature is 80°F, the CDD would be 15. If this happened 10 times in a year the annual CDD would be 150. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. CDD projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP). RCP 4.5 is a stabilization scenario where total radiative forcing is stabilized around 2050 by employment of a range of technologies and strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. The dataset is shown in degrees Celsius (°C) at a spatial resolution of 0.25°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset provides projections on how temperature patterns are likely to change in the coming decades and how this may affect future energy demands. For example, CDDs are often used as a proxy to estimate energy requirements for cooling buildings. This dataset improves the accessibility of climate data by summarizing global climate information and providing the information as an open dataset in a common geospatial format. 

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). The NEX-GDDP dataset is intended to assist the scientific community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Cooling Degree Days dataset was created with temperature data from NEX-GDDP. The NEX-GDDP datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, NEX-GDDP extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Sheffield et al. (2006)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/jcli/article/19/13/3088/30860/Development-of-a-50-Year-High-Resolution-Global) dataset as historical reference.  

The annual CDD for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using NEX-GDDP data on a per-pixel basis. Daily CDDs were calculated by subtracting the baseline temperature of 65°F from daily average temperature values. If the daily average temperature was below 65°F, it was counted as zero. Then, annual CDD was calculated by summing all daily CDD values over a given year. Annual CDDs were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. The baseline average was then subtracted from each of the nine projected decades to create the projected change in cooling degree days.

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the CDD in 2000 is actually an average of the annual CDDs between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association. Additionally, units were converted from the original dataset units (Kelvin) to °C.

title: [TEST] World Database on Protected Areas -- Global
Annual Internal Displacement from Conflict
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset tracks the number of people who have been internally displaced due to conflict worldwide each year. Internal displacement refers to the forced movement of people within the country they live in. Millions of people are forced to flee their homes each year due to conflict, violence, development projects, disasters, and climate change and remain displaced within their countries of residence.
  
  

Internally displaced persons (IDPs) can include both citizens and other habitual residents of the country, such as stateless persons. IDPs from conflict can include, but are not limited to
  
  
- families caught between warring parties who had to flee their homes due to continuous attacks or threats; and
  
  
- families pushed to leave their homes by constant harassment by local criminal gangs.
  
  

Some of the typical needs and protection risks that arise in internal displacement include family separation, loss of documentation, loss of property, and further exposure to the risk of continued displacement.
  
  

This dataset is produced by the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC) with the aim of informing policy and operational decisions in order to reduce the risk of future displacement and improve the lives of IDPs worldwide. Resource Watch also shows IDMC estimates of the number of people displaced annually due to [natural disasters](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore?zoom=3&lat=-2.110674954311376&lng=7.456691250000007&basemap=dark&labels=light&layers=%255B%257B%2522dataset%2522%253A%2522ef9945f7-d934-4a88-a02a-570f14fffefc%2522%252C%2522opacity%2522%253A1%252C%2522layer%2522%253A%25223bda62f1-7146-4dd5-bf3f-d3bfae26d0d7%2522%257D%255D&page=1&sort=relevance&sortDirection=-1&search=soc.062a) at the national level, as well as [recent internal displacement from conflict, natural disasters, and development](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore?zoom=3&lat=-2.110674954311376&lng=7.456691250000007&basemap=dark&labels=light&layers=%255B%257B%2522dataset%2522%253A%2522d2f6245d-5b9b-4508-874b-d42a2be7d058%2522%252C%2522opacity%2522%253A1%252C%2522layer%2522%253A%25222059a368-b4f1-4c30-b874-b41e49c3c5e4%2522%257D%255D&page=1&sort=relevance&sortDirection=-1&search=soc.062c), which are monitored in near real-time and displayed on an event-by-event basis.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
After IDMC learns that displacement due to conflict has occurred, it conducts situational monitoring within certain countries. At the end of the year, it reports the total number of people displaced in each country. For each event, information from a wide variety of different sources is compiled, generating the most comprehensive and reliable displacement estimate. These sources include national and subnational government authorities, UN agencies and other international organizations, related global databases, civil society organizations, news media outlets, and other entities. description: CO-OPS has been involved with tsunami warning and mitigation since the Coast & Geodetic Survey started the Tsunami Warning System in 1948 to provide warnings to the Hawaiian Islands. After the December 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, CO-OPS was tasked to coordinate with the NOAA Tsunami Warning Centers in upgrading existing stations with new Data Collection Platform (DCP) and communications technology and with expanding the tsunami warning capabilities of the NWLON. Work began in 2005 to upgrade 33 existing water level sand install 16 new stations from the Pacific Ocean to the Caribbean Sea by October 2006. The National Geophysical Data Center (NGDC) serves as the archive center for this data and provides the historical data to users.

description:
### Overview  
  
The Saltmarshes dataset displays the distribution of saltmarshes globally, drawing from occurrence data (surveyed and/or remotely sensed). The dataset captures location data for saltmarsh in 99 countries worldwide. The data were collected from 1973 to 2015, with most occurring after 2005.

  
  
Saltmarshes are highly productive ecosystems that are rich in biodiversity and underpin the estuarine food web. In particular, saltmarshes serve as nesting, nursery and feeding grounds for numerous species of birds, fish, molluscs and crustaceans. Saltmarshes are extremely valuable but often overlooked ecosystems, contributing to livelihoods locally and globally through the associated ecosystem services they provide, including fish production, carbon storage, and coastal protection. Despite their importance, saltmarsh areas are declining around the world, having lost between 25% and 50% of their global historical coverage ([Crooks et al. 2011](https://openknowledge.worldbank.org/bitstream/handle/10986/18318/605780REPLACEM10of0Coastal0Wetlands.pdf), [Duarte et al. 2008](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12237-008-9038-7)). Vast areas have been lost through conversion to agriculture, urban and industrial land, while remaining saltmarshes face many other current and potential threats ([Gedan et al. 2009](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.marine.010908.163930)).

  
  
In light of increasing anthropogenic and environmental pressures on coastal ecosystems, global data on the occurrence and extent of saltmarshes are needed to draw attention to these critical ecosystems and the benefits they generate for people. The dataset was developed to establish a mapped baseline inventory of the extent of the global distribution of saltmarshes. The data aim to support resource management, strengthen decision-making, and facilitate tracking of progress towards global conservation targets set by multilateral environmental agreements. The UN Environment Programme World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC) collated and integrated the dataset with support from Conservation International and The Nature Conservancy.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The Saltmarshes dataset consists of data derived from peer-reviewed articles and [grey literature](https://www.greylit.org/about), including reports and databases created by governmental and non-governmental organisations, universities, institutes and researchers globally. Data in the original source materials were collected using remote sensing and field-based survey methods. Data quality ranges from high-resolution maps to low-resolution representations, with the scale varying from 1:10,000 to 1:4,000,000, with most falling within the 1:10,000 to 1:100,000 range. Data contributors were asked to submit metadata with each dataset to provide the contextual information important for informing analyses. Saltmarshes were identified in accordance with definitions provided by data sources, where available, or were determined using expert opinion (available in the supplementary material).The precautionary principle was applied to ensure consistency across designations: if the authors were uncertain about the classification of the habitat, it was not included. Please refer to the supplementary material and associated [metadata](https://data.unep-wcmc.org/pdfs/43/WCMC_027_Global_Distribution_of_Saltmarsh.pdf?1617122640) from the authors for more information regarding each data source presented.

  
  
 For the full documentation, please see the source [publication](https://doi.org/10.3897/BDJ.5.e11764).

description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](5c5e654e-182b-4ab4-8a3c-edff79cc68ea) as a replacement.**_
  
This data set, a collaboration between the GLAD (Global Land Analysis & Discovery) lab at the University of Maryland, Google, USGS, and NASA, measures areas of tree cover loss across all global land (except Antarctica and other Arctic islands) at approximately 30 × 30 meter resolution. The data were generated using multispectral satellite imagery from the Landsat 5 thematic mapper (TM), the Landsat 7 thematic mapper plus (ETM+), and the Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager (OLI) sensors. Over 1 million satellite images were processed and analyzed, including over 600,000 Landsat 7 images for the 2000-2012 interval, and more than 400,000 Landsat 5, 7, and 8 images for updates for the 2011-2017 interval. The clear land surface observations in the satellite images were assembled and a supervised learning algorithm was applied to identify per pixel tree cover loss.  
  

In this data set, “tree cover” is defined as all vegetation greater than 5 meters in height, and may take the form of natural forests or plantations across a range of canopy densities. Tree cover loss is defined as “stand replacement disturbance,” or the complete removal of tree cover canopy at the Landsat pixel scale. Tree cover loss may be the result of human activities, including forestry practices such as timber harvesting or deforestation (the conversion of natural forest to other land uses), as well as natural causes such as disease or storm damage. Fire is another widespread cause of tree cover loss, and can be either natural or human-induced.  
  

This data set has been updated five times since its creation, and now includes loss up to 2017 (Version 1.5). The analysis method has been modified in numerous ways, including new data for the target year, re-processed data for previous years (2011 and 2012 for the Version 1.1 update, 2012 and 2013 for the Version 1.2 update, and 2014 for the Version 1.3 update), and improved modelling and calibration. These modifications improve change detection for 2011-2017, including better detection of boreal loss due to fire, smallholder rotation agriculture in tropical forests, selective losing, and short cycle plantations. Eventually, a future “Version 2.0” will include reprocessing for 2000-2010 data, but in the meantime integrated use of the original data and Version 1.5 should be performed with caution. Historical Coral Bleaching Stress Frequency
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset shows the frequency and intensity of heat stress events. Heat stress events can be detected using sea surface temperature (SST), which is the water temperature close to the ocean's surface. A heat stress event occurs when the SST near coral reefs exceeds the historical baseline for that area. This dataset describes the number of heat stress events and the average period of time between them during 1985-2018 at a 5 kilometer (km) resolution. 

  
  
Stress events are defined by applying Coral Reef Watch's [Degree Heating Week (DHW) methodology] (https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/satellite/education/tutorial/crw24_dhw_product.php) at coral reef-containing and adjacent satellite pixel locations worldwide. The DHW attempts to capture both the level of abnormal heating and its duration: 1 DHW is equivalent to 1 week of SST 1°C above the expected summertime maximum at a given location. The three thresholds for heat stress in this dataset correspond to occurrence (DHW>0), significant coral bleaching (DHW≥4), and widespread bleaching and significant mortality (DHW≥8).

  
  
SST and its fluctuations are critical to ecosystem dynamics and health, as many marine organisms can thrive only within certain temperature ranges. In particular, research indicates that a coral reef’s “thermal history” is among the most important factors influencing its ability to withstand heat stress events. Accordingly, with support from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) [Coral Reef Conservation Program](http://coralreef.noaa.gov/), [Coral Reef Watch (CRW)] (https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/satellite/index.php) developed a variety of thermal history metrics for coral reef management, initially released in July 2014. The metrics were derived from CRW's Version 3.1 [CoralTemp daily global 5 km (1/20°) satellite SST data product] (https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/product/5km/index_5km_sst.php), for the period 1985-2018. 

  
  
Coral reef sites that have experienced fewer heat stress events may have natural protection from exposure to conditions conducive to bleaching (e.g., strong mixing, upwelling). However, corals at those sites may also be more sensitive to heat stress, resulting in higher impacts if a stress event does occur. Alternatively, sites that have been regularly exposed to heat stress can have a reduced sensitivity, and therefore lower impact from the stress.

  
  
Coral reefs are among the most biologically rich and productive ecosystems on earth and provide valuable ecosystem benefits to millions of people in coastal areas. They are, however, widely threatened by both local threats (such as overfishing, pollution, and direct physical damage) and the global threats of ocean warming and acidification. These have already caused widespread damage to most of the world’s coral reefs, resulting in reduced areas of living coral, increased algal cover, diminished species diversity, and lower fish abundance, as well as degraded economic and social benefits to many coastal communities.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
Stress events are defined for 1985-2018 by applying CRW's Degree Heating Week (DHW) methodology at pixel locations worldwide that either contained coral reefs or were adjacent to pixels that did. SST input data were drawn from the [CoralTemp daily global 5 km satellite SST data product (Version 3.1)](https://coralreefwatch.noaa.gov/product/5km/index_5km_sst.php), which represents the nighttime ocean temperature measured at the surface. The source data for CoralTemp are a combination of the:
  
  
1. NOAA/National Environmental Satellite, Data, and Information Service (NESDIS) operational near real-time daily global 5 km Geostationary-Polar-orbiting (Geo-Polar) Blended Night-only SST Analysis;
  
  
2. NOAA/NESDIS 2002-2016 reprocessed daily global 5 km Geo-Polar Blended Night-only SST Analysis; and the
  
  
3. 1985-2002 daily global 5 km night-only SST reanalysis produced by the United Kingdom Met Office, on the Operational SST and Sea Ice Analysis (OSTIA) system.

  
  
NOAA's daily global 5 km Geostationary-Polar Blended Night-only SST Analyses (both the near real-time and reprocessed products) utilize sensors from multiple geostationary and polar-orbiting satellites to derive a global SST data field at a resolution of 5 km (1/20°). The few remaining gaps are filled using optimal interpolation through space and time.

  
  
Heat stress will build up if the temperature around corals rises and stays above the bleaching threshold (1°C above the highest summertime mean SST). The DHW is the product of the deviation above this threshold and the length of time it persists. This captures not only how far the temperature is above the threshold, but how long it has stayed above that point. Thus the DHW shows how much heat stress has accumulated in an area over the past 12 weeks. It is a running sum: as time advances one half-week (a timestep), a half-week timestep "falls off" the back end of the 12-week window.

  
  
For the full documentation, please click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. Additional data about heat stress frequency, heat stress onset, SST variability, SST trends, climatology, and annual SST history are available from the data provider. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.

title: Total Suspended Matter
description:
### Overview  
  
The Total Suspended Matter (TSM) dataset shows the concentration of inorganic particulate matter in seawater in grams per cubic meter (g/m³). The specific data products shown on Resource Watch originate with the [Ocean Land Color Instrument](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/user-guides/sentinel-3-olci) B (OLCI B), a sensor carried by the [Sentinel-3B satellite](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/missions/sentinel-3). An equivalent product for Sentinel-3A is available from the provider. This monthly and 8-day global products have a resolution of 1/24 degrees (°) at the equator (about 4.63 kilometers); between the two satellites, the time series run back to 2016. Like all similar [GlobColour datasets](https://www.globcolour.info/products_description.html), monthly and 8-day "Level-3" TSM is derived from the accumulated data of the daily [Level-2 product](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-3-olci/level-2/ocean-processing) across that month. In the case of TSM, the monthly values represent a simple average of the daily values.

  
  
TSM is a measure of turbidity: the haziness of a liquid due to suspended particles. Runoff water can carry clay, silt, and other matter from land into the ocean. As the turbidity of water increases, it becomes denser and less clear due to a higher concentration of these light-blocking particles. This in turn can have a wide variety of effects including: reduced sunlight reaching plants and animals, affecting the growth of plankton; increased water temperatures and altered transportation of heat through the water column; and decreased visibility.

  
  
Ocean color is an "essential climate variable" needed to support the carbon cycle monitoring requirements of the [UNFCCC (United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change)](http://unfccc.int/2860.php). It is also a climate variable that cannot be globally monitored without using satellite observations. In order to cover the long time span necessary for climate monitoring purposes, the required ocean color dataset can only be built by merging together observations made with different satellite systems. The GlobColour project started in 2005 to provide a continuous dataset of merged [Level-3 Ocean Colour](https://www.globcolour.info/CDR_Docs/GlobCOLOUR_PUG.pdf) products. Merging outputs from different sensors ensures data continuity, improves spatial and temporal coverage, and reduces data noise.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The monthly, Level-3 TSM product represents an average of the constituent Level-2 inputs, as is the 8-day TSM product. The [ocean processing](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-3-olci/level-2/ocean-processing) component of OLCI Level-2 processing is dedicated to handling water pixels. It is divided into two main tasks: atmospheric correction and ocean color processing. 

  
  
Atmospheric correction follows two approaches; the "standard" or "baseline" approach, further split into atmosphere characterisation and correction, and an "alternative" approach in which atmospheric parameters and water-leaving reflectances are inverted through dedicated neural networks. TSM is produced via the latter.

  
  
One output of the ocean color processing is a set of bio-geophysical products, including TSM, derived from the water-leaving reflectance (and associated error) using a neural net; these products are particularly focused on more complex Case 2 waters (typically along coasts) in which additional constituents must be considered (scattering by total suspended matter as well as absorption by detrital and Gelbstoff material).

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://sentinel.esa.int/web/sentinel/technical-guides/sentinel-3-olci/level-2/ocean-processing), as well as the [Product User Guide](https://www.globcolour.info/CDR_Docs/GlobCOLOUR_PUG.pdf).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. In addition to monthly TSM, GlobColour also offers daily and 8-day versions. GlobColour generates similar Level-3 (merged Level-2) products for a large number of biological parameters, such as particulate inorganic carbon and primary production, as well as atmospheric and ocean optical parameters. Collectively these are too numerous to list here. The full set can be found in the [Product User's Guide](https://www.globcolour.info/CDR_Docs/GlobCOLOUR_PUG.pdf).  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team reformatted this dataset before displaying it on Resource Watch. See the documentation on how Resource Watch processed the data on [Github](https://github.com/resource-watch/nrt-scripts/tree/master/ocn_011_nrt_rw0_total_suspended_matter).

Maritime Boundaries
description:
### Overview  
  
The Maritime Boundaries dataset shows boundaries for exclusive economic zones (EEZs), territorial seas (TS) and contiguous zones (CZ) for coastal countries around the world. The [United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS)](http://www.vliz.be/en/imis?module=ref&refid=325469) defined the EEZ, CZ and TS maritime boundaries and coastal baselines. An EEZ is a sea zone over which a country has special rights to explore and use marine resources. Typically, a country’s EEZ extends 200 nautical miles (NM) from its coast (or baseline), unless that distance would overlap with another country’s EEZ. TS are coastal waters that are the sovereign territory of a given country. This zone extends a maximum of 12 NM from a country’s baseline. A CZ is a sea zone that extends an additional 12 NM beyond the outer edge of the TS (up to 24 NM from a country’s baseline). Countries have limited legal rights within the CZ. Data for the Maritime Boundaries dataset was published by the Flanders Marine Institute (VLIZ) in 2019 and is available for download from [Marine Regions](https://marineregions.org/). 

  
  
The Maritime Boundaries dataset is a useful tool for managing and displaying marine data. It provides a standardized map of global maritime boundaries. The Maritime Boundaries dataset is useful for linking marine information, such as species distribution lists or coral reef health, to particular countries. The dataset also shows the various jurisdictional reaches of countries. This is important for understanding marine resource management and the rights that countries have to protect their waters. 

  
  
The Maritime Boundaries dataset was generated by the [Flanders Marine Institute (VLIZ)](https://www.vliz.be/en), a non-profit organization dedicated to scientific research on the ocean, seas, coasts and tidal estuaries. Based in Belgium VLIZ was established in 1999 by the Flemish government and [the Research Foundation - Flanders](https://www.fwo.be/en/). The central focus of VLIZ is to provide knowledge to the research community, educators, the general public, policymakers and marine industries.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The boundaries shown in the Maritime Boundaries dataset were generated from a combination of **normal**, **straight** and **archipelagic** baselines. The UNCLOS defines a **normal** baseline as the low-water line along a country’s coast. A **straight** baseline is a straight line representing the baseline where there is a fringe of islands along the coast, or the coast is heavily indented. **Archipelagic** baselines apply to archipelago countries, which are made of a group of islands. These baselines are straight lines that connect the coastlines and contain the main islands of the country. Normal baselines were drawn using a combination of the [Esri Countries 2014 dataset](https://www.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=ac80670eb213440ea5899bbf92a04998) and the [United Nations Environmental Program (UNEP) Coral Reef Distribution dataset](https://data.unep-wcmc.org/datasets/1), referred to as the World Countries 2014 dataset. Coral reef data was used to draw baselines for countries where reefs were a fundamental part of their maritime boundaries. Straight and archipelagic baselines were drawn based on [definitions from the UN](https://www.un.org/Depts/los/LEGISLATIONANDTREATIES/regionslist.htm) or maritime treaties and agreements. Countries typically define borders at sea in agreements with their neighbors. These borders were used when available. Median lines were drawn between countries where borders at sea were not specified. Median lines connect points at equal distance from neighboring coastal countries.

  
  
The baselines were used to generate boundaries of EEZ, TS and CZ sea zones. The boundaries are seaward distances of 200 EEZ, 12 TS and 24 CZ NM from a country’s baseline. Polygons representing the EEZ, TS and CZ areas were calculated using a buffer distance measured from the combination of straight, archipelagic and normal baselines. The Maritime Boundaries dataset was created by merging the EEZ, TS and CZ boundaries with the World Countries 2014 dataset using the [Pairwise Dissolve tool](https://pro.arcgis.com/en/pro-app/tool-reference/analysis/pairwise-dissolve.htm) in ESRI ArcGIS Pro 2.5.0. Landlocked countries were removed before merging and added in afterward. Differences between coastlines in the EEZ and World Countries 2014 datasets caused small gaps in the polygons. These gaps were fixed in QGis 3.0 using the [Delete Holes tool](https://docs.qgis.org/3.10/en/docs/user_manual/processing_algs/qgis/vectorgeometry.html#delete-holes) and the [Difference tool](https://docs.qgis.org/3.10/en/docs/user_manual/processing_algs/qgis/vectoroverlay.html#difference).  

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.marineregions.org/eezmethodology.php).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. VLIZ also provides boundaries of internal waters, archipelagic waters and high seas. For access to the full dataset and additional information, click the “Learn more” button.

Extreme Precipitation Days
description:
Extreme precipitation days represent the annual average count of days with precipitation greater than the 99th percentile of the baseline, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). 

The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100.

The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run).

The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm 
 
PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

description:
The Gridded Livestock of the World Version 3, produced by the Food and Agriculture Organization and the University of Oxford, shows the distribution of eight livestock animal densities in animals per square kilometer at a spatial resolution of 5 arcminutes. The animals include cattle, water buffalo, horse, sheep, goats, pigs, chickens and ducks.   
  

The Gridded Livestock of the World (GLW) created two versions of their data for two different methods of distributing livestock census weighting: area weighting and dasymetric weighting. Resource Watch displays the dasymetric weighting data, and the metadata refers to this methodology. More information can be found in the Cautions section.    
  

The total livestock census numbers for administrated levels are found by mining agricultural yearbooks or through direct contacts with ministries or statistical bureau. The livestock numbers are then distributed within census polygons according to weights established by a Random Forest model using high resolution spatial covariates including population, vegetation health, and climate. 
In compiling subnational census counts, priority is given to censuses that most closely match the reference year, 2010, and those with the highest level of spatial detail. This results in a global mosaic of data from different spatial resolutions and different years. Both the spatial resolution and year of census data depend on the country and species in question. See cautions section and source publication for more information.  Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. description:
_**This dataset has been archived, and we will no longer be updating or maintaining it. We recommend using [this dataset](3b6f853a-622d-4fff-827c-901b5b4352b0) as a replacement.**_
  
The traffic deaths rate data produced by the World Health Organization (WHO) give mortality data from road traffic injuries. To estimate road traffic fatal injury, countries were classified into 4 groups as follows: (1) Countries with death registration data completeness of at least 80%. For this category, one of the following data points was used: death registration, projection of the most recent death registration, reported death, or projected reported deaths. (2) Countries with other sources of information on cause of death. This group includes India, Iran, Thailand, and Vietnam. For these countries, a regression method was used to project forward the most recent year for which an estimate of total road traffic deaths was available. (3) Countries with population less than 150,000 and without eligible death registration data. For these countries, the deaths reported in the survey were used directly, without adjustment. (4) Countries without eligible death registration data. For these countries, a negative binomial regression model was used. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. This data set, released by the UN Environment Programme's World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC), shows of the global distribution of cold-water corals that inhabit the colder deep waters of continental shelves and offshore canyons, ranging from 50 to over 1,000 m depths. They lack zooxanthellae and may build reef-like structures or occur solitarily. Occurrence records are given for the subclass Octocorallia (octocorals; also known as Alcyonaria) and 4 Orders (in Class Anthozoa): Scleractinia (reef-forming corals), Antipatharia (black corals), Zoanthidae (encrusting or button polyps), and Pennatulacea (sea pens). Occurrence records are also available for the order sub-Order Filifera (lace corals) in Class Hydrozoa. Depth range, including upper and lower depths, status of the sample, and reference to where the record was first published, is also included. This data set contains data for 132 countries and comprises 32,631 occurrences of cold corals, including locations within the high seas. Occurrence records were obtained from various sources, including reports, peer-reviewed articles, and expert consultations. Many individuals and organizations contributed by providing UNEP-WCMC with their data in electronic form. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. title: Air Quality: Black Carbon Estimated Emissions
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) shows global anthropogenic emissions of black carbon in 2018 from the following sectors: agriculture, power generation, residential, ship, road transportation, off-road transportation, and industrial processes. The dataset also includes a layer for the sum of all sectors, as total emissions.  
  
Black carbon is a particulate emitted from the incomplete combustion of fossil fuels, biofuels, and biomass. Major [sources include](https://www.c2es.org/document/what-is-black-carbon/) diesel engines, coal-fired power plants, cook stoves, wood burning, and forest fires. According to the [U.S. Environmental Protection Agency](https://www.epa.gov/air-research/black-carbon-research), black carbon is a “global environmental problem that has negative implications for both human health and our climate.”  
  
Inhalation of black carbon is associated with [cardiovascular disease, respiratory problems, cancer, and even birth defects](https://www.epa.gov/air-research/black-carbon-research). Black carbon makes up a significant portion of particulate matter pollution.  
  
Although black carbon is not a greenhouse gas, it contributes to climate change in a few ways. Its dark color absorbs solar radiation, which warms up the atmosphere. Black carbon also settles on snow and ice, darkening these surfaces that would normally reflect a lot of solar radiation. According to research published in [Nature Geoscience](https://www.nature.com/articles/ngeo473), black carbon may have caused more than 30% of the recent rapid warming in the Arctic.  
  
Resource Watch also shows CAMS global anthropogenic emissions data for [nitrogen oxides (NOₓ)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/249cb5ff-0ad1-461c-bcaa-15fb44f45d72), [methane (CH₄)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/85936c69-b773-458b-90c4-b47d5d3b5f0d), and [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/92cb0e3c-369e-4c66-908c-5723f608e35b). Each compound shows the emissions by sector for up to 11 sectors, depending on the atmospheric compound. The CAMS global anthropogenic emissions dataset was developed by Emissions of Atmospheric Compounds and Compilation of Ancillary Data (ECCAD-AERIS). The data has global coverage at a 0.1 degree resolution, which is approximately 11 kilometers x 11 kilometers at the equator, but [changes with distance](https://www.thoughtco.com/degree-of-latitude-and-longitude-distance-4070616) from the equator. Emissions are provided as an annual sum for the years 2000 to 2019. This dataset shows annual emissions for the year 2018.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The CAMS global anthropogenic emissions are based on the data provided by the Community Emissions Data System (CEDS) and Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research version 4.3.2 (EDGARv4.3.2) historical data. In preparing the dataset, the 0.5 degree global CEDS emissions dataset for the years 2011 to 2014 was used to calculate a linear trend in emissions. These trends were then disaggregated onto the same 0.1 degree grid as in EDGARv4.3.2. The sectors were then merged and aligned between the CEDS and EDGARv4.3.2 datasets. The 2011 to 2014 trends were applied to the EDGARv4.3.2 2010 emissions to estimate the emissions up to the year 2018. For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://atmosphere.copernicus.eu/sites/default/files/2019-05/cams_emissions_general_document_apr2019_v6.pdf).  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch also shows CAMS global anthropogenic emissions data for [nitrogen oxides (NOₓ)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/249cb5ff-0ad1-461c-bcaa-15fb44f45d72), [methane (CH₄)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/85936c69-b773-458b-90c4-b47d5d3b5f0d), and [sulfur dioxide (SO₂)](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/92cb0e3c-369e-4c66-908c-5723f608e35b).

title: India Projected Change in Precipitation
description:
This dataset, available from the Centre for Climate Change Research (CCCR) at the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM), shows projected change in precipitation over the Indian subcontinent. 

These downscaled climate scenarios contain high resolution downscaled projections of regional climate and monsoon over South Asia until 2100 for the IPCC using the International Centre for Theoretical Physics (ICTP) Regional Climate Model (RegCM4) at 50 km horizontal resolution. The projections are an ensemble of six member global climate models from the CMIP5, which help drive the regional model with lateral and lower boundary conditions. The IITM-RegCM4 regional climate model outputs are archived by CCCR-IITM in the framework of the WCRP regional activity Coordinated Regional Climate Downscaling Experiment (CORDEX; http://www.cordex.org), and are disseminated to users and stakeholders for application studies and impact assessments by publishing on the CCCR-IITM Earth System Grid Federation (ESGF) data node (see more details at http://cccr.tropmet.res.in/home/cordexsa_datasets.jsp).

Projected change in precipitation is computed using daily precipitation in kilograms per square meter per second for the historical period (1951-2005) and for future projections (2006-2099) based on two Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) scenarios (RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5) of the IPCC. These indicators are then used to derive an ensemble mean (average of the 6 IITM-RegCM4 model members). These are presented as the future changes in three 30-year period: short-term (2016-2045), mid-term (2036-2065), and long-term (2066-2095) averages relative to the baseline 30-year period (1976-2005) average.

The daily fields from 1951 to 2099 for each member model available in netCDF4 file format are processed to compute the climate indicators (30-year averages) using the Climate Data Operators (CDO; https://code.mpimet.mpg.de/projects/cdo), which is a collection of command line operators to manipulate and analyze climate model data. The processed climate indicators available in netCDF4 file format can be visualized using the Grid Analysis and Display System (GrADS; http://cola.gmu.edu/grads), an interactive desktop tool that is used for easy access, manipulation, and visualization of earth science data.

title: wps_011_urbanization
Female Management of Agricultural Holdings
description:
### Overview  
  
This dataset describes the percentage of female agricultural holders out of total agricultural holders in 104 countries. The dataset is based on the most recently available survey data per country between1990 and 2012. It shows the extent of how often women have responsibility and management control in agriculture. An agricultural holding is an economic unit under single management engaged in agricultural production activities, without regard to title, legal form, or size. An agricultural holder is the person who makes major decisions regarding the use and management of an agricultural holding. This is a useful concept to understand issues related to agricultural productivity and responsibilities in production.

  
  
Having accurate land management data that is disaggregated by sex is essential in developing clear policy responses to inequalities facing women in rural areas. Increasing the quantity of female agricultural holders is integral in reducing food scarcity.

  
  
This dataset is one of the five indicators from the Gender and Land Rights Database (GLRD), an online platform that was launched by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO). The indicators are used to highlight political, legal and cultural determinants that affect the achievement of women’s land rights globally. FAO collaborated with and adopted a framework developed by the International Food Policy Research Institute Policies, Institution, and Markets (IFPRI - PIM) to build comparable indicators of land ownership and management across the globe. 
  
  
### Methodology  
  
  
  
This dataset was calculated using the following formula: 

  
  
( Female agricultural holders  / total agricultural holders ) * 100 

  
  
Data sources mainly comprised agricultural censuses carried out by National Statistics Offices and/or Ministries of Agriculture.  Agricultural censuses are typically carried out every 10 years. Data for European countries came from Eurostats. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](http://www.fao.org/3/a-i4862e.pdf).

title: Trawling Activity
description:
### Overview  
  
The Apparent Fishing Effort dataset, produced by Global Fishing Watch (GFW), shows the distribution of time spent fishing in different locations throughout the ocean at a 0.01 degree resolution between 2012 and 2021. The time spent fishing in each pixel is tracked using a maritime Automatic Identification System (AIS).

  
  
Commercial fishing is a vital part of the global economy and is crucial to the food security and cultural identity of millions of people. However some practices, like trawling and dredging, destroy far more ocean habitat than any other fishing practice. When dredging or trawling, commercial vessels drag a dredge or heavy net, respectively, along the seafloor to scrape up species like oysters or shrimp. The process of scraping the seafloor is extremely destructive to deep-sea marine ecosystems, productivity, biodiversity, and carbon storage. Historically, practices like trawling and dredging have been difficult and costly to monitor, but technology and transparency are driving tangible change in how the sector is managed. 

  
  
Global Fishing Watch is advancing ocean governance through increased transparency of human activity at sea. By creating and publicly sharing map visualizations, data and analysis tools, they enable scientific research and drive a transformation in how we manage our ocean. By 2030, they aim to monitor and visualize the impact of ocean-going vessels, both industrial and small-scale, that are responsible for the vast majority of the global seafood catch.

  
  
### Methodology  
  
Global Fishing Watch’s apparent fishing effort dataset is based on transmissions broadcast using publicly available automatic identification system (AIS) information. AIS is a GPS-like device that large ships use to broadcast their position in order to avoid collisions. Each year, more than 400,000 AIS devices broadcast vessel location along with other information on vessel identity, course and speed. Ground stations and satellites pick up this information, meaning a ship’s movements can be followed even in the most remote parts of the ocean. 

  
  
GFW uses two convolutional neural networks (CNN)—a cutting edge form of machine learning model—to help classify fishing vessels (vessel characterization model) and predict when they are fishing (fishing detection model). They first [identify fishing vessels](https://globalfishingwatch.org/datasets-and-code-vessel-identity/) by combining a comprehensive database of vessel registry information with the output of the vessel characterization model to predict features like geartype and size. Next, GFW estimates where and when each vessel is fishing based on its movement patterns. The fishing detection model was trained using over a thousand manually labeled vessel tracks to learn what fishing movements look like. This model predicts a score for every AIS position in the database to distinguish fishing positions from non-fishing positions, such as during vessel transits. When the fishing detection model scores an AIS position as a fishing position, the time associated with that AIS position is considered apparent fishing activity. For more information about the two models, please see the supplementary materials of the [associated paper](https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.aao5646).

  
  
After identifying fishing vessels and detecting fishing positions in the AIS data, apparent fishing effort can be calculated for any area by summarizing the fishing hours for all fishing vessels in that area. Global Fishing Watch’s fishing detection algorithm is a best effort mathematically to identify “apparent fishing activity.” As a result, it is possible that some fishing activity is not identified as such by Global Fishing Watch; conversely, Global Fishing Watch may show apparent fishing activity where fishing is not actually taking place. 

  
  
 To generate maps of apparent fishing effort GFW “rasterizes” the AIS positions by placing them into a grid and calculating the total fishing activity in each grid cell. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.aao5646)
  
  
### Additional Information  
  
Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. This map displays effort by trawlers or dredgers. Resource Watch shows separate GFW fishing effort data [for all other vessels](https://resourcewatch.org/data/explore/11f16cb9-def0-4bd5-a60e-50c542b837e3). [Data disaggregated by flag state, vessel, and gear type](https://globalfishingwatch.org/data-download/datasets/public-fishing-effort) is also available through Global Fishing Watch. 

  
  
For access to the full dataset and additional information, click on the “Learn more” button.
  
  
### Visualizing the Data  
  
Our team requested a visualization of the data through the Global Fishing Watch API. This visualization powered by 4-Wings, Global Fishing Watch experimental technology for rapid access to global
scale temporal data sets. See the documentation on how Resource Watch retrieved the data on [Github.](https://github.com/resource-watch/data-pre-processing/tree/master/com_030c_rw1_trawling_activity)

title: National Infant Mortality
description:
The 'mortality rate, infant (per 1,000 live births)' dataset released by the World Bank data catalog is the number of infants dying before reaching one year of age, per 1,000 live births in a given year.  The main sources of mortality data are vital registration systems and direct or indirect estimates based on sample surveys or censuses. A "complete" vital registration system - covering at least 90 percent of vital events in the population - is the best source of age-specific mortality data. Estimates of neonatal, infant, and child mortality tend to vary by source and method for a given time and place. Years for available estimates also vary by country, making comparisons across countries and over time difficult. To make neonatal, infant, and child mortality estimates comparable and to ensure consistency across estimates by different agencies, the United Nations Inter-agency Group for Child Mortality Estimation (UN IGME), which comprises the United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF), the World Health Organization (WHO), the World Bank Group, the United Nations Population Division, and other universities and research institutes, developed and adopted a statistical method that uses all available information to reconcile differences. The method uses statistical models to obtain a best estimate trend line by fitting a country-specific regression model of mortality rates against their reference dates. title: Air Quality: Population Exposed to Unhealthy Levels of Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5)
description:
### Overview  
  
The Population Exposed to Unhealthy Levels of Fine Particulate Matter (PM2.5) dataset shows the percentage of a country’s population living in places with unhealthy levels of PM2.5 in the air. Particulate matter (PM) are air pollutants such as dirt, dust, soot or smoke. The [EPA categorizes](https://www.epa.gov/pm-pollution/particulate-matter-pm-basics) PM by size. Pollutants that are 10 micrometers or smaller in diameter can be inhaled by humans and can be harmful to human health. Fine particulate matter (less than 2.5 micrometers in diameter) poses a greater health risk than PM10. The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines state that ambient air concentrations exceeding 10 micrograms of PM2.5 per cubic meter (m3) are unhealthy. Estimates of annual PM2.5 concentrations were generated by combining data from atmospheric chemistry transport models, satellite observations of aerosols in the atmosphere and ground-level particulate monitoring. These estimates were then overlain with gridded population data. This data was collected globally at the country level for select years between 1990 and 2017.

  
  
PM2.5 occurs in many shapes and chemical compositions. Some particulates are emitted directly from a source, such as construction sites or smokestacks. Others are created from complex reactions in the atmosphere. Cooking and heating with solid fuel sources, such as coal, wood or dung, creates harmful smoke and particulate matter. Around 40% of the world’s population relies on solid fuels for cooking and heating. The small size of PM2.5 allows particulates to get deep into the lungs and even into the bloodstream. [Scientific studies](https://www.thelancet.com/gbd?source=post_page) have linked particulate pollution exposure to various health problems including lung cancer, heart disease and respiratory disease. People with heart or lung diseases, children, and older adults are most likely to be affected by particulate pollution exposure. The [Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study](http://www.healthdata.org/gbd/2019) estimates that air pollution causes 6.5 million deaths every year. PM2.5 also negatively affects the environment causing haze, acid rain and damage to sensitive forests or farm crops. Additionally, air pollution can hinder development for low and middle-income countries and vulnerable populations. 

  
  
This dataset is part of the GBD study, an international scientific effort led by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation at the University of Washington. The World Bank Group commissioned the first GBD study as part of its 1993 World Development Report. The GBD believes that everyone deserves to live a long, healthy life. Their study aims to help achieve this by providing a dataset to improve health systems and eliminate disparities. A consortium of more than 3,600 researchers from more than 145 countries contributed to the GBD study. The WHO was a major contributor as well. The study quantifies the health effects of diseases and injuries and analyzes the risk factors for death and disease. Air quality is among the study’s 84 environmental, behavioral, occupational and metabolic risk factors.
  
  
### Methodology  
  
This dataset was derived from a gridded model of air quality and population. Estimates of annual PM2.5 concentration were generated by combining data from three sources: atmospheric chemistry transport models, [satellite observations of aerosols](http://fizz.phys.dal.ca/~atmos/martin/?page_id=140) in the atmosphere, and ground-level particulate monitoring. [Harvard University’s GEOS Chem](http://acmg.seas.harvard.edu/geos/) atmospheric chemistry model was used to simulate atmospheric transport of chemical air pollutants such as organic carbon, nitrate, sulfate, ammonium and mineral dust. Atmospheric aerosol observations collected by National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) satellites were combined with the GEOS Chem model to estimate atmospheric particulate concentration. Data was available at a resolution of 0.1 degrees (°). Ground-level particulate monitoring data for PM10 and PM2.5 concentrations were also used. This data was measured by 9,960 ground monitors in 108 countries. Air quality data from each of the three measurements was calibrated by country and modeled using a hierarchical statistical method.

  
  
The GBD used high resolution population data from NASA’s [Gridded Population of the World](https://beta.sedac.ciesin.columbia.edu/data/collection/gpw-v4) (GPW) dataset. The GPW data was upscaled from its resolution of 0.0417° to fit the GBD’s model grid cell sizes of 0.1°. GPW data was then overlaid with gridded PM2.5 estimates to determine the percentage of a country’s population living in an area with unhealthy air quality. The WHO’s definition of unhealthy air quality are air concentrations greater than 10 micrograms of PM2.5 per m3. In grid cells where PM2.5 concentrations exceeded this threshold, the population data was summed and divided by the country’s total population. The data from all grid cells was aggregated by population-based weighted averaging to calculate each country’s population percentage figure. 

  
  
For the full documentation, please see the source [methodology](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(18)32225-6/fulltext#supplementaryMaterial) (supplementary appendix 1, page 67).

title: Dry Spells
description:
Dry spells represent the annual average count of 5-day periods without precipitation, as derived from the NASA Earth Exchange Global Daily Downscaled Projections (NEX-GDDP). 

The NEX-GDDP data set is comprised of downscaled climate scenarios for the globe that are derived from the General Circulation Model (GCM) runs conducted under the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5) and across two of the four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios known as Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs). The CMIP5 GCM runs were developed in support of the Fifth Assessment Report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC AR5). The NEX-GDDP data set includes downscaled projections for RCP 4.5 (referred to as “Low Emissions” on PREPdata) and RCP 8.5 (referred to as “High Emissions” on PREPdata) from the 21 models and scenarios for which daily scenarios were produced and distributed under CMIP5. The two RCPs correspond to different levels of radiative forcing due to greenhouse gas emissions. RCP 4.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions peak at 2040 and then decline, while RCP 8.5 refers to a future scenario where emissions continue to rise through 2100.

The NEX GDDP data set contains daily maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2100. The spatial resolution of the data set is 0.25 degrees (~25 km x 25 km). The NEX-GDDP data set is provided to assist the science community in conducting studies of climate change impacts at local to regional scales, and to enhance public understanding of possible future global climate patterns at the spatial scale of individual towns, cities, and watersheds. Each of the climate projections includes monthly averaged maximum temperature, minimum temperature, and precipitation for the periods from 1950 through 2005 (Retrospective Run) and from 2006 to 2099 (Prospective Run).

The NEX-GDDP data was processed for inclusion on PREPdata. This processing included deriving climate indicators from the raw temperature and precipitation data and then using those indicators to create an ensemble measure of the 21 climate models, as well as their 25th and 75th percentiles. The data is presented at two different temporal resolutions: decadal averages and 30-year period averages. A detailed explanation of the data processing can be found here: https://colab.research.google.com/drive/15_fPbKvuRsBKUWlrOWXurUDllzRJmMVd#scrollTo=mPL4beQdNjDm 
 
PREPdata shows the processed data derived from the NEX GDDP data set. For access to the original NEX GDDP data set and additional information, see the Download from Original Source link. If you are interested in obtaining the processed data, please contact us.

title: Oil Palm Concessions
description:
### Overview  
  
The Oil Palm Concessions dataset shows public lands allocated by governments to private companies for industrial-scale oil palm plantations. The dataset is a compilation of concession data from Cameroon, Indonesia, Liberia, Malaysia, Papua New Guinea, Republic of the Congo and the Solomon Islands. Concession name, company and area in hectares (ha) are included in the Oil Palm Concessions dataset. Oil Palm Concessions data is typically from government agencies or nonprofits, although the data source and date vary by country. The Oil Palm Concessions dataset is updated monthly. 

  
  
Palm oil is an edible vegetable oil produced from the fruits of the oil palm tree. According to the [World Wildlife Fund (WWF)](https://www.worldwildlife.org/industries/palm-oil), oil palm is a highly productive crop and grows only in tropical regions. Palm oil does not require refrigeration and is used in food products, cosmetics and detergents. However, oil palm farming contributes to deforestation and the release of harmful greenhouse gases into the atmosphere. [According to a study from the European Commission](http://pure.iiasa.ac.at/id/eprint/14868/), oil palm farming is responsible for 8% of global agriculture-related deforestation. Deforestation from oil palm farming is most prevalent in Indonesia, Brazil and Malaysia. Deforestation has many harmful impacts on the environment, including habitat destruction, erosion, air pollution and groundwater contamination. Understanding the locations and extent of oil palm plantations provides information about potential environmental impacts. It can also be used to encourage farmers and businesses to use sustainable farming practices. 

  
  
The Oil Palm Concessions dataset was generated by [Global Forest Watch (GFW)](https://www.globalforestwatch.org/about/), an organization established in 1997 by the [World Resources Institute](https://www.wri.org/). WRI is an independent, non-governmental global research organization which seeks to create equity and prosperity through sustainable natural resource management. They provide data and research about climate, energy, food, forests, water, cities and oceans. GFW uses satellite data and cloud computing to monitor deforestation in near real-time. This information is critical to ending illegal deforestation and fires, and promoting sustainable practices. It can be used by business owners and the public to monitor the environmental impacts of activities like logging, mining and farming. Additionally, farmers and landowners can use this data to protect their land and resources.  
  
### Methodology  
  
The term “oil palm concession” refers to an area allocated by a government to a company for industrial-scale oil palm plantations. GFW generated the Oil Palm Concessions dataset by compiling concession data from Cameroon, Indonesia, Liberia, Malaysia, Papua New Guinea, Republic of the Congo and Solomon Islands. Most locations in the dataset include the company, concession name and concession area (ha). 

  
  
Data for each country was collected from various sources, including from government agencies and public documents. The most common source was maps from forestry or agriculture-specific government agencies. Data from the public domain (company websites, news reports, NGOs) was used for countries where data was not readily available from government agencies. This data was used to create polygons representing the locations and boundaries of concessions. Additional information such as company and concession name was added to the polygons as attributes. The Oil Palm Concessions dataset was published in 2019, though the exact dates vary by country. Concession data for each country is available on the [GFW Open Data Portal](https://data.globalforestwatch.org/search?q=oilpalm).

title: Projected Cumulative Precipitation U.S. (RCP4.5)
description:
The Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation in the United States (U.S.) dataset shows the change in annual average total precipitation at ten year intervals between 2000 and 2080, compared to a baseline time period of 1960-1990. The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the total precipitation in 2000 is actually an average of the cumulative precipitation between the years 1985 and 2015. Precipitation projections are based on the future greenhouse gas emission rates determined by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s (IPCC’s) Representative Concentration Pathways (RCP) 8.5. RCP 8.5 is a hypothetical scenario where there is no decrease in greenhouse gas emission rates within the 21st century. Cumulative average precipitation is divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change. Values greater than 1 indicate that cumulative precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that the number is decreasing. Data is presented at a spatial resolution of 0.0625°.

The increase in global greenhouse gas concentrations, and resulting change in climate, is set to fundamentally alter our relationship with the planet, impacting agriculture, infrastructure, disaster management, and human conflict. In order to anticipate and adapt to these changes, the Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation dataset provides projections on how precipitation patterns are likely to change in the coming decades. Precipitation changes are projected to be more varied across the world, generally showing increases in mean precipitation in high-latitude regions and a pole-ward shift of subtropical arid regions. In addition, precipitation is projected to occur in fewer, but more intense events. Except in the few areas that are projected to see substantial drying, historically extreme precipitation events are expected to become more frequent worldwide. Even as precipitation increases, dry periods are projected to increase in length and frequency. 

This dataset has been processed by Vizzuality and the World Resources Institute using [Local Constructed Analogs](https://gdo-dcp.ucllnl.org/downscaled_cmip_projections/) (LOCA) projections for the continental United States. LOCA datasets are intended to provide access to climate and hydrologic projections to assess potential climate change impacts, regional climate projections, and policy responses to climate risk. A previous version of this dataset was processed and produced by the [Partnership for Resilience and Preparedness (PREP)](https://prepdata.org/), aiding in PREP’s mission to build resilience to climate change by improving access to climate data.

The Projected Change in Cumulative Precipitation dataset was created with precipitation data from LOCA. LOCA datasets were derived from Global Circulation Model (GCM) experiments that were produced for the [Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Fifth Assessment Report (AR5)](https://www.ipcc.ch/site/assets/uploads/2018/05/SYR_AR5_FINAL_full_wcover.pdf). These experiments, known as the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project phase 5 (CMIP5) included results from climate models designed to simulate climate under different levels of greenhouse gas concentrations.  

CMIP5 data include a large number of models (45), climate scenarios (4), years (150+), and variables (20-40). Even at its coarse resolution (1-4°) this results in billions of layers. By downscaling, LOCA extracts only the data they require and reduces the overall size of the data, using the [Livneh et al. (2015)](https://www.nature.com/articles/sdata201542) dataset as historical reference.

The cumulative precipitation for each year, climate model, and scenario was calculated using LOCA data on a per-pixel basis. This was done by adding all daily precipitation data over a given year. The cumulative precipitations were then combined into 31-year averages for the baseline time period of 1960-1990 and nine periods centered on the start of each decade from 2000 to 2080. Then each of the nine projected decades were divided by the baseline average to calculate the projected change in cumulative precipitation. Values greater than 1 indicate that cumulative precipitation is increasing, while values less than one indicate that cumulative precipitation is decreasing.

The data shown at each ten year interval represents a 31-year average, centered around the indicated year. For example, the cumulative precipitation in 2000 was calculated as an average of the cumulative precipitation between the years 1985 and 2015. 31-year averages were chosen because they minimize the effects of annual and decadal variation and highlight the long-term climate signal. The baseline period was selected to align with longstanding guidance from the World Meteorological Association.

description:
This dataset, created by the Global Land Analysis and Discovery (GLAD) lab at the University of Maryland and supported by Global Forest Watch, is the first Landsat-based alert system for tree cover loss. While most existing loss alert products use 250 m resolution MODIS imagery, these alerts have a 30 m resolution and thus can detect loss at a much finer spatial scale. The alerts are currently operational in the tropics. New Landsat 7 and 8 images are downloaded as they are posted online at USGS EROS, assessed for cloud cover or poor data quality, and compared to the 4 previous years of Landsat-derived metrics (including ranks, means, and regressions of red, near infrared, and shortwave infrared bands, and ranks of NDVI, NBR, and NDWI). The metrics and the latest Landsat image are run through decision trees to calculate a median probability of forest disturbance. Pixels with probability > 50% are reported as tree cover loss alerts. For more information on methodology, see the paper in Environmental Research Letters. Alerts remain unconfirmed until 2 or more loss observations occur out of 4 observations or within 180 days. Alerts that remain unconfirmed after subsequent observations are removed from the data set. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the dataset. description:
The Global Surface Water data set contains maps of the location and temporal distribution of surface water from 1984 to 2015 and provides statistics on the extent and change of those water surfaces. These data were generated using 3,066,102 scenes from Landsat 5, 7, and 8 acquired between March 16, 1984, and October 10, 2015. Each pixel was individually classified into water/nonwater using an expert system, and the results were collated into a monthly history for the entire time period and 2 epochs (1984-1999, 2000-2015) for change detection. The mapping layers product consists of 1 image containing 7 bands. It maps different facets of the spatial and temporal distribution of surface water over the last 32 years. Areas where water has never been detected are masked. Resource Watch shows only a subset of the data set. For access to the full data set and additional information, see the Learn More link.

The Subnational Human Development Index (SHDI) was constructed by the Global Data Lab (GDL) at the Institute for Management Research at Radboud University (RU). The index is a measure of the average subnational values for three dimensions of subnational human development: education, health, and standard of living for the period 1995-2019.

This dataset was translated from the United Nations Development Programme’s (UNDP) official Human Development Index (HDI) to the subnational level using subnational values retrieved from the Area Database of the Global Data Lab, national statistical offices, and the EU statistical office (Eurostat). The Global Grid of Probabilities of Urban Expansion to 2030 by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration Socioeconomic Data and Applications Center (NASA SEDAC) presents spatially explicit probabilistic forecasts of global urban land cover change from 2000 through 2030 at a 2.5 arc-minute resolution. For each grid cell that is nonurban in 2000, a Monte Carlo model assigned a probability of becoming urban by the year 2030. The authors first extracted urban extent circa 2000 from the NASA MODIS Land Cover Type Product, Version 5, which provides a conservative estimate of global urban land cover. The authors then used population densities from the Global Rural-Urban Mapping Project, Version 1 (GRUMP v1), to create the population density driver map. They estimated the amount of new urban land in each UN region by 2030 in a Monte Carlo fashion based on present empirical distribution of regional urban population densities and probability density functions of projected regional population and GDP values for 2030.
